{
  "content":"# 311 — Integration tests & run output (`last-run.json`)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nPhase 2 writes a `last-run.json` after every map run, recording per-\nbox invocations, inputs, outputs, and any errors. The editor reads\nit to display a run summary. Phase 2 testing is ad-hoc: a few maps\nin `maps/` (`hello`, `branch-test`, `classify-demo`, `driver-test`)\nthat the developer runs by hand to verify the synchronous executor\nstill works.\n\nPhase 3 changes the shape of the problem: many concurrent\ninvocations, possibly thousands per run when iterators are in play,\nwritten from multiple worker threads. The phase 2 \"build a single\ntable at end of run\" approach does not survive that. And the\nexisting maps cover only a small slice of the new surface (no\nqueued inputs, no large iterator counts, no fan-in).\n\nThis issue covers two things that go together: the format and\nwriter for the run output, and the integration test plan that\nexercises the phase 3 runtime end-to-end.\n\n## Part A — Run output\n\n### Decoupling from the editor\n\nThe editor (phase 2) is being scoped down to a pure map editor — it\ndoes not know how to run maps and does not display run results.\n`last-run.json` is therefore not a UI feed. It exists for:\n\n- LLM consumption — agents reading the file to understand what a\n  run did\n- CLI-driven inspection — a future viewer utility (out of scope\n  here) that pretty-prints the file\n- Test harness consumption — the integration tests below diff the\n  written file against expected output\n\nDecoupling means the writer's design is driven by these consumers,\nnot by editor rendering needs.\n\n### File format: JSON Lines\n\nThe phase 2 single-document format does not work when the runner is\nstreaming events from many threads. Use JSON Lines instead — one\nJSON object per line, each line is one event, the file grows\nmonotonically as the run proceeds.\n\nEvent types:\n\n```jsonl\n{\"event\":\"run_start\", \"ts\":1234567890.123, \"map\":\"maps/classify-demo\", \"n_workers\":16}\n{\"event\":\"task_submit\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"box_id\":\"classify\", \"worker_idx\":-1}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3, \"duration_us\":127, \"output_size\":12}\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5, \"size\":256, \"n_cells\":1}\n{\"event\":\"slot_free\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5}\n{\"event\":\"run_end\", \"ts\":..., \"duration_us\":1850, \"n_tasks\":7}\n```\n\nJSONL is append-only, which makes thread-safe writing tractable: a\nsingle mutex around the write call serializes the lines, and each\nline is self-contained so a partial line on crash is recoverable\n(reader skips the broken trailing line).\n\nThe reader (LLM, viewer, test harness) parses one line at a time;\ntotal file size doesn't have to fit in memory.\n\n### What gets logged\n\nPer-task: submission, start, end, duration, output size. Inputs\nand outputs are NOT logged by default — for iterator boxes\nproducing thousands of invocations, logging every value bloats\nthe file unbounded. There is a verbosity switch:\n\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — log inputs and outputs (truncated past\n  some byte limit, e.g. 4 KB) per task. For debugging.\n- Default: log task lifecycle but not values.\n\nSlot allocator events (alloc, free, coalesce, grow) at a separate\nverbosity level. Off by default; on under `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`.\nFor diagnosing memory issues.\n\n### Writer mechanism\n\nA single dedicated writer thread inside the runner consumes events\nfrom a multi-producer single-consumer ring buffer. Worker threads\npush event records (small fixed-size structs) into the ring; the\nwriter pulls them, serializes to JSON, and writes lines to the\nfile. This avoids per-event mutex contention — the ring buffer is\nthe only shared state, and a well-written MPSC ring is lock-free\non the producer side.\n\nAlternative considered: each worker writes its own log file, merge\nat end. Simpler concurrency, but readers would have to merge by\ntimestamp — and any cross-event reasoning (was task A still\nrunning when task B ended?) requires the merge anyway.\n\nThe writer thread is started after the pool is created and joined\nbefore `pool_destroy`. It also handles `run_end` as the very last\nevent, including the final summary.\n\n### File location\n\n`<map-dir>/last-run.jsonl` (note: `.jsonl` not `.json` — the\nextension reflects the format change). Overwritten on every run.\n\nA rotated archive (`last-run.jsonl.1`, `.2`, …) is out of scope.\nUsers who want history copy the file before re-running.\n\n## Part B — Integration tests\n\n### Scope\n\nEnd-to-end tests of the pool runner against real map directories.\nEach test is:\n\n1. A map directory under `tests/maps/<name>/`\n2. An expected `last-run.jsonl` (or a comparison spec) under\n   `tests/expected/<name>.jsonl`\n3. A test driver script that runs the map and diffs\n\nThe test driver is `scripts/run-tests.sh`. It iterates\n`tests/maps/`, runs each, diffs against expected (with a normalizer\nthat drops timestamps, durations, worker indices — anything non-\ndeterministic), and reports pass/fail.\n\n### Test maps\n\nCoverage targets:\n\n| Test map                  | What it exercises                                    |\n|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|\n| `hello`                   | Single Lua box, one input, one output                |\n| `data-only`               | Data box → call box. No inputs, just stored values   |\n| `fan-out-3`               | One output → three consumer boxes (peek, refcount)   |\n| `fan-in-iterator`         | Three producers → iterator with queued input         |\n| `comparator-routing`      | Comparator with all three branches (lt/eq/gt)        |\n| `iterator-100`            | Iterator with 100 input values, round-robin to 3 paths |\n| `multilang`               | One Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all wired      |\n| `large-output`            | Box producing a 1 MB string (variable-size heap)     |\n| `cycle-detector-fail`     | Non-iterator cycle — load must abort                 |\n| `missing-input-fail`      | Connection references a nonexistent box — load aborts|\n| `box-error-fail`          | Box function returns nonzero — runner aborts         |\n\nThe `*-fail` tests verify error behavior — the runner is expected\nto exit nonzero with a precise error message. The driver matches\nexit code and stderr against expected.\n\n### Test driver\n\n```bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh\nfor test_dir in tests/maps/*/; do\n    name=$(basename \"${test_dir}\")\n    expected=\"tests/expected/${name}.jsonl\"\n\n    actual=$( \"${SOURCE_DIR}/soramech-pool\" \"${test_dir}\" )\n    rc=$?\n\n    if [ -f \"${expected}.exit\" ]; then\n        # *-fail tests: assert exit code and stderr substring\n        check_failure \"${name}\" \"${rc}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\"\n    else\n        # success tests: diff normalized last-run.jsonl\n        check_success \"${name}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\" \"${expected}\"\n    fi\ndone\n```\n\n`normalize_jsonl` strips timestamps, durations, worker indices,\nslot ids, and task ids (all non-deterministic) and sorts events by\nevent type. The result should be deterministic across runs.\n\n### Phase 3 demo map\n\nA single map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` that\ndemonstrates everything working together:\n\n- Multiple entry-point data boxes\n- Lua, C, and Bash boxes all wired together\n- An iterator with a queued input\n- A comparator routing into different downstream paths\n- A large-output box (variable-size heap)\n- Non-trivial graph topology (≥ 10 boxes)\n\nRun with `./run.sh` from the demo directory. Prints a short summary\nof what happened (parsing the `last-run.jsonl`) so the demo is\nvisible without a viewer utility.\n\nThis satisfies the standing project rule (CLAUDE.md) that each\nphase produces a runnable demo in `issues/completed/demos/`.\n\n### Test infrastructure constraints\n\n- Tests must not depend on the editor or any HTTP server\n- Tests must not depend on internet access\n- Tests must run in under 60 seconds total on a developer machine\n- Tests must be deterministic when normalized (any\n  non-determinism is normalized out, not papered over with retries)\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Whether to log inputs/outputs by default. Useful for development,\n  noisy for production. Current decision: opt-in via env var,\n  default off.\n- Slot-event logging: also opt-in. Useful for diagnosing memory\n  issues. Off by default.\n- File format: JSON Lines is the choice. An alternative was a\n  protobuf or msgpack binary log, which is faster to write but\n  harder to inspect by hand. JSONL wins on inspectability.\n- Whether to keep timestamps as Unix epoch floats or ISO 8601\n  strings. Epoch floats are smaller and easier to diff. Stick with\n  floats.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n### Run output (Part A)\n1. Define the event struct and JSONL line format. Start with\n   `run_start`, `task_start`, `task_end`, `run_end`.\n2. Implement the MPSC ring buffer for events.\n3. Implement the writer thread: pulls from ring, serializes,\n   appends a line to the output file.\n4. Wire event emission into the pool runner: `run_start` at\n   startup, `task_start` and `task_end` in the dispatch action,\n   `run_end` after quiescence.\n5. Add the verbosity env vars and the optional event types.\n\n### Tests (Part B)\n6. Create `tests/maps/` and `tests/expected/` directory structure.\n7. Write the `hello` test as the first end-to-end smoke check.\n8. Write the test driver `scripts/run-tests.sh` and the JSONL\n   normalizer.\n9. Add tests one at a time as each runtime feature lands. The\n   `*-fail` tests can land before their corresponding successful\n   tests if the failure path is implemented first.\n10. Build the phase 3 demo map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/`\n    once the rest of phase 3 is implemented.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — test driver (to be written)\n- `tests/maps/`, `tests/expected/` — test fixtures (to be created)\n- `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` — phase 3 demo (to be built)\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — emits run_start / run_end\n- `src/dispatch.c` — emits task_start / task_end\n- `src/slot-store.c` — emits slot_alloc / slot_free (verbose mode)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot events\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task lifecycle events\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — load-time errors\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — `make test` invokes this\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — blocking semantics relevant to\n  test design\n",

Ten queued\ninputs means the iterator task visits the queue ten times, advancing the\ncounter and firing a different output path each time.\n\n### Blocking semantics for long-running operations\n\nThe pool's parallelism comes from running N worker threads concurrently\non N cores. Each worker is sitting inside a single dispatch task at any\ngiven moment. If a box function does something that takes a long time —\n`sleep`, blocking I/O, a synchronous network request, waiting on a long-\nrunning subprocess — **the worker thread is occupied for the full\nduration**. It cannot pick up other tasks while it waits.\n\nConcretely:\n- 16-worker pool, 1 box sleeping 10 seconds → the other 15 workers\n  continue normally.\n- 16-worker pool, 16 boxes all sleeping → all workers parked, no other\n  task runs until a sleep finishes.\n- The pool size is also the budget for \"blocking activities\". Heavy\n  use of `sleep`-style boxes means raising `SORAMECH_WORKERS`.\n\nWhy the runtime does not have a scheduler: SoraMech is deliberately not\nin the business of \"park this task and wake it at time T.\" There is no\ndelayed-spawn primitive, no timer thread, no polling loop. Adding one\nwould mean a second concurrency model alongside the pool, with its own\nsynchronization story. Instead, we lean on the pool's existing\nmechanism: a task either runs (occupying a worker) or is blocked on a\nslot waiting for a value (parked, no worker held). Long sleeps are an\n\"occupying a worker\" case.\n\nFor users who need many concurrent waits without burning workers, the\ngraph-level pattern is cooperative: split the operation into \"kick off\nthe thing\" (returns immediately) and \"check whether the thing is done\"\n(returns immediately, returns a status), and wire them through an\niterator with a queued input. The iterator polls. No individual box\nblocks for long. Each box completes quickly, freeing its worker.\n\nThis is a documented constraint, not a bug. Box authors should know\nthat an unbounded `sleep` inside a function is the equivalent of\nholding a worker hostage. **309 — Build system & Makefile orchestration**:

- Vendoring policy: copied source, no submodules, with `VENDOR.md` per directory
- Spec discovery at runtime: runner reads `/proc/self/exe`, finds `langs/` next to itself; `SORAMECH_LANGS_DIR` overrides
- macOS `.dylib`/`_NSGetExecutablePath` flagged in open questions

**310 — Priority queue: wired in, no-op behaviorally**:
- Every `pool_spawn` passes `SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT = 1`; `SM_MAX_PRIORITY = 1`

Test driver normalizes timestamps, durations, worker indices, slot/task IDs out and diffs against expected JSONL.

1	# SoraMech — Architecture
2	
3	## Three programs, one data format
4	
5	SoraMech is three independent programs that share a common on-disk format:
6	the map directory. None of the three knows about the others at runtime.
7	
8	```
9	  Browser (index.html)
10	       |  HTTP (file CRUD)
11	       v
12	  soramech-server.lua          [map directory]
13	                               maps/<name>/
14	                                 boxes/
15	                                 data/
16	                                 drivers.json
17	                                 meta.json
18	                                 tmp/ -> /tmp/<name>/
19	       ^
20	       | reads & writes
21	  soramech-runner.lua
22	```
23	
24	### soramech-server.lua
25	
26	Thin HTTP proxy. Receives JSON requests from the browser and translates
27	them into file reads and writes on the map directory. No logic beyond
28	path validation and basic consistency checks (e.g., reject a delete if
29	the box is still referenced by another box's connection list).
30	
31	Started with: `luajit soramech-server.lua <maps-root> [port]`
32	Default port: 7700
33	
34	Endpoints (all operate on map files):
35	  GET  /maps                        list maps
36	  GET  /maps/<name>/boxes           list box IDs
37	  GET  /maps/<name>/boxes/<id>      read box file
38	  PUT  /maps/<name>/boxes/<id>      write box file
39	  DELETE /maps/<name>/boxes/<id>    remove box (validates no dangling refs)
40	  GET  /maps/<name>/data/<name>     read data file
41	  PUT  /maps/<name>/data/<name>     write data file
42	  GET  /maps/<name>/drivers         read drivers.json
43	  PUT  /maps/<name>/drivers         write drivers.json
44	  GET  /maps/<name>/meta            read meta.json
45	
46	### soramech-runner.lua
47	
48	FSM execution engine. Loads a map directory, validates the graph, then
49	executes boxes in dependency order. Each box invocation is wrapped in a
50	`task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` call — matching the 3d-rts thread pool's
51	action chain signature for future threading compatibility.
52	
53	Started with: `luajit soramech-runner.lua <map-dir>`
54	
55	Execution steps:
56	  1. Read all box files from boxes/
57	  2. Validate: all connection endpoints exist, branch "else" handled
58	  3. Determine entry box from meta.json
59	  4. Execute: resolve inputs, invoke driver, collect outputs, fire wires
60	  5. On completion, write last-run snapshot to tmp/last-run.json
61	
62	### index.html
63	
64	Static HTML + vanilla JS. Infinite-scroll canvas. Box diagram editor.
65	Talks to soramech-server.lua for all file operations. No run button —
66	the user starts the runner separately from the terminal.
67	
68	## Map directory format
69	
70	```
71	maps/<name>/
72	  meta.json          — { name, description, entry_box_id }
73	  drivers.json       — { ".lua": "drivers/lua.sh", ".c": "drivers/c.sh", ... }
74	  boxes/
75	    <id>.json        — one file per box (see Box file format below)
76	  data/
77	    <name>.json      — lua table as JSON; sections have "constant": bool
78	  drivers/
79	    lua.sh           — built-in lua driver (shipped with soramech)
80	    c.sh             — built-in C driver
81	    bash.sh          — built-in bash driver
82	  tmp/               — symlink to /tmp/<name>/
83	    last-run.json    — snapshot of last run (ephemeral)
84	    logs/            — run logs
85	    cache/           — compiled binaries (C driver cache)
86	```
87	
88	## Box file format
89	
90	```json
91	{
92	  "id": "unique-string",
93	  "label": "Human name",
94	  "kind": "call",
95	  "ref": "src/strings.lua",
96	  "fn": "trim",
97	  "inputs": [
98	    { "name": "text", "type": "string" }
99	  ],
100	  "outputs": [
101	    { "name": "result", "type": "string" }
102	  ],
103	  "connections": [
104	    {
105	      "from_box": "unique-string",
106	      "from_output": "result",
107	      "to_box": "next-box-id",
108	      "to_input": "text"
109	    }
110	  ],
111	  "ui": { "x": 120, "y": 340 }
112	}
113	```
114	
115	For branch boxes (`"kind": "branch"`):
116	```json
117	{
118	  "id": "classify",
119	  "kind": "branch",
120	  "inputs": [{ "name": "value", "type": "string" }],
121	  "ports": [
122	    { "name": "rogue", "predicate": { "op": "eq", "value": "rogue" } },
123	    { "name": "wizard", "predicate": { "op": "eq", "value": "wizard" } },
124	    { "name": "else" }
125	  ],
126	  "connections": [...]
127	}
128	```
129	
130	Connections are written to BOTH endpoint box files. The runner validates
131	at load time that both ends agree. Disagreement is a hard error.
132	
133	## Language driver interface
134	
135	Drivers are shell scripts. The engine invokes them as:
136	
137	  <driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [<arg1> <arg2> ...]
138	
139	The single return value is encoded as a JSON value on stdout. Exit code
140	non-zero = box failure. Each box has exactly one output wire — multi-return
141	tuples are not supported (see docs/003-driver-system.md).
142	
143	## Execution model (v1 — synchronous)
144	
145	The runner walks the graph depth-first from the entry box. Each box call:
146	
147	  1. Collect inputs: read wired output values from predecessor boxes
148	  2. Invoke driver: shell out to the appropriate driver script
149	  3. Collect output: decode single JSON value from driver stdout
150	  4. Store output: held in runner memory, keyed by box id (one value per box)
151	  5. Fire connections: enqueue boxes whose input dependencies are now met
152	
153	Each step is wrapped in a `task_fn` boundary so the runner can be
154	threaded later by substituting the synchronous executor with one backed
155	by the 3d-rts custom thread pool. The intermediate path is coroutine-based
156	non-blocking I/O before the full thread pool is integrated.
157	
158	## Data files
159	
160	Persistent data lives in data/<name>.json. Format:
161	
162	```json
163	{
164	  "constant": false,
165	  "fields": {
166	    "history": [],
167	    "config": { "constant": true, "value": { "model": "soramind-default" } }
168	  }
169	}
170	```
171	
172	Top-level `constant: true` makes the whole file read-only. Individual
173	fields can be flagged constant within an otherwise mutable file.
174	
175	Ephemeral state (scratch tables, logs, last-run snapshot) goes to tmp/,
176	which is a symlink to /tmp/<map-name>/. It survives the run but not a
177	reboot — intentionally.
178	
```

2	
3	## Phase 1 — Foundation
4

12	- Run `luajit soramech-runner.lua <map-dir>` and have it execute the map
13	- Write a custom language driver and have the runner use it

17	  102 — language driver interface
18	  103 — runner: graph loader and validator
19	  104 — runner: synchronous executor (task boundary)
20	  105 — HTTP server: file CRUD API
21	  106 — web editor: canvas and box rendering
22	  107 — web editor: wiring and connection UI
23	  108 — branch box and predicate routing

28	box, reads a data file, writes an output. The browser shows the same map
29	visually with correct wiring drawn.

31	## Phase 2 — Concurrent execution
32	
33	Goal: boxes whose inputs are all satisfied fire concurrently.
34	
35	- Coroutine-based non-blocking executor: the ready-queue becomes a
36	  coroutine scheduler; boxes yield while waiting on upstream results
37	- Cross-language calls use Unix domain socket servers (one per language
38	  runtime per worker), non-blocking on the Lua side via LuaSocket
39	- Multiple maps running concurrently share nothing (separate processes)
40	- Integration path toward the 3d-rts custom thread pool: the coroutine
41	  scheduler and task boundary are designed to swap in the thread pool
42	  without changing the box execution model
43	
44	## Phase 3 — SoraMind integration
45	
46	Goal: boxes that call SoraMind inference endpoints on the Alpine cluster.
47	
48	- LLM call box type: sends a prompt, receives a completion string
49	- Prompt assembly: text values wired from upstream boxes, data file
50	  sections explicitly loaded into prompt context
51	- Branch box connected to an LLM classifier: "rogue, wizard, or else"
52	- Else port retry with pseudo-randomized temperature parameter
53	- Streaming output from SoraMind inference back to the runner
54	
55	## Phase 4 — Map-to-map calls
56	
57	Goal: a box that invokes another map as a subroutine.
58	
59	- Map call box type: specifies another map directory, passes inputs,
60	  receives outputs
61	- Maps can run concurrently with each other
62	- Entry/exit contracts defined in meta.json
63	
64	## Phase 5 — Remote runner
65	
66	Goal: run a map on the Alpine cluster, edit it from a laptop.
67	
68	- Runner process on a remote machine (Alpine node)
69	- Server on the same machine exposes map files over HTTP
70	- Browser editor on the laptop connects to the remote server
71	- Results written to remote data files, accessible via server
72

1	# SoraMech — Language Driver System
2	
3	## What a driver is
4	
5	A driver is a shell script. It knows how to invoke a function in one
6	language. The runner knows nothing about any language — it looks up the
7	file extension in drivers.json, finds the driver script, and calls it.
8	
9	Lua and C ship with pre-written driver scripts. They are not special
10	cases in the runner. They use exactly the same interface a user-written
11	driver uses. If you want to call a Haskell function or a Rust function,
12	write a driver script and add the extension to drivers.json.
13	
14	## Driver contract
15	
16	The runner invokes a driver as:
17	
18	  <driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [<arg> ...]
19	
20	Arguments are always strings. Structured values (tables, arrays) are
21	passed as JSON strings and must be decoded by the driver before use.
22	
23	The driver must:
24	  - Exit 0 on success, non-zero on failure
25	  - Print a single JSON value to stdout on success (string, number,
26	    boolean, object, or null) — one output wire per box
27	  - Print an error message to stderr on failure (runner captures and logs
28	    it)
29	
30	Nothing else. No side channels. The runner reads stdout, decodes the JSON
31	value, and passes it to all wired downstream inputs.
32	
33	Note: multi-output tuple returns are not supported. Each box has exactly
34	one output wire. If multiple values need to travel together, encode them
35	as a JSON object or array and decode downstream.
36	
37	## Shell script vs. binary caller
38	
39	Two kinds of refs exist in a box file:
40	
41	  "ref": "src/strings.lua",  "fn": "trim"
42	      → source caller. runner looks up ".lua" in drivers.json and
43	        invokes the driver with file + fn + args.
44	
45	  "ref": "src/trim.sh"       (no "fn")
46	      → binary caller. runner invokes the script directly with just
47	        the args. The script is its own driver. Stdout is parsed as
48	        JSON as with a normal driver.
49	
50	Binary callers include compiled binaries too: if the ref ends in a
51	binary extension or has no extension, the runner execs it directly.
52	
53	## Built-in driver scripts
54	
55	Shipped in a global drivers/ directory alongside soramech-runner.lua.
56	Maps can override any driver by defining the same extension in their
57	local drivers.json pointing at a map-local script.
58	
59	### drivers/lua.sh
60	
61	Invokes a single function from a Lua file using luajit. The function
62	must be a module-level export (returned from the file or set in a
63	package). Args are decoded from JSON; return values are encoded to JSON.
64	
65	### drivers/c.sh
66	
67	Compiles the .c file if its mtime is newer than the cached binary in
68	tmp/cache/. The cache key is the source file's absolute path hashed.
69	Invokes the compiled binary with the args. The binary must follow the
70	driver output contract (JSON to stdout).
71	
72	The binary is expected to expose a `main`-style entry that reads args
73	from argv and writes JSON to stdout. A small C header (shipped with
74	soramech) provides helpers for this.
75	
76	### drivers/bash.sh
77	
78	Invokes a bash function defined in the .sh file by sourcing the file
79	and calling the function with the args as positional parameters.
80	The function must echo a JSON value (or array) to stdout.
81	
82	## User-defined drivers
83	
84	Add the file extension and path to the map's drivers.json:
85	
86	  { ".rs": "drivers/rust.sh" }
87	
88	Write drivers/rust.sh. It receives the same arguments as any built-in
89	driver. Compile, interpret, or delegate however the language requires.
90	The runner doesn't care.
91	
92	## Driver lookup order
93	
94	  1. Map-local drivers.json (maps/<name>/drivers.json)
95	  2. Global drivers.json (alongside soramech-runner.lua)
96	  3. Hard error if extension not found — no fallback, no silent skip
97	
98	## Passing structured values between boxes
99	
100	All inter-box values are JSON at the transport layer. Inside a Lua box,
101	dkjson decodes input strings to Lua tables. The driver re-encodes return
102	values to JSON. Inside a C box, the shipped helper header decodes argv
103	JSON strings to C structs and encodes results back.
104	
105	This means structured values cross language boundaries cleanly: a Lua
106	table produced by one box can be consumed by a C function in the next
107	box, because both sides see JSON at the wire level.
108	
```

7	Effil-jit is explicitly NOT used. It has been removed from all docs and issues.
8	
9	Threading roadmap:
10	1. **Now**: Synchronous executor. Single-threaded, sequential box execution.
11	2. **Next**: Coroutine-based non-blocking executor. LuaSocket non-blocking I/O + coroutine scheduler. Boxes yield while waiting on cross-language socket calls.
12	3. **Eventually**: 3d-rts custom thread pool. The `task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` boundary in `src/004-executor.lua` is the designed swap point.
13	
14	Cross-language IPC direction: Unix domain socket servers (one per language runtime per worker thread). Not temp files, not anonymous pipes. The socket servers are persistent subprocesses — one per language per thread, idle-blocked on `accept()`.
15	
16	**Why:** Effil was considered but rejected. The 3d-rts thread pool is the target. No date set.
17	
18	**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC, do not suggest effil. Reference the 3d-rts pool as future work and coroutines as the intermediate path.
19	
```

1	---
2	name: SoraMech project context
3	description: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and north star use case for SoraMech
4	type: project
5	originSessionId: 2029ad16-5678-4b15-931f-3f52d826597a
6	---
7	SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.
8	
9	**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.
10	
11	**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**
12	- `soramech-server.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy only. No runner management. Started for remote editing.
13	- `soramech-runner.lua` — FSM execution engine, invoked from CLI independently. Reads map dir, walks graph, invokes drivers.
14	- `index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only, no "run" button. Talks to server for file ops.
15	
16	**Key architecture decisions:**
17	- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; runner validates both ends agree — hard error if not.
18	- Language drivers are shell scripts. No special cases for any language in the runner. Lua/C/bash ship as pre-written driver scripts, same interface as user-defined ones.
19	- Driver invocation: `<driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [args...]`. Outputs JSON to stdout.
20	- Branch box: dedicated node kind with named output ports + always an "else" port. LLM-based "else" can be unwired (triggers retry of upstream box with pseudo-randomized retry_vary fields). Numeric/string "else" must be wired or map won't start.
21	- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua` library (not a built-in runner API).
22	- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Logs, last-run snapshot, C binary cache go here.
23	- v1 executor: synchronous, each box call wrapped in `task_fn(inputs)->outputs` boundary matching 3d-rts thread pool action chain signature for future swap.
24	
25	**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract.
26	
```

1	# 210 — Comparator wire branching
2	
3	## Status
4	
5	open
6	
7	## Supersedes
8	
9	The original design of this issue described an `llm-route` box kind that used an
10	Ollama call to route between named output ports. That design has been removed:
11	the `llm-route` box kind, the executor's `llm_route_call` helper, and all
12	related inspector and wire rendering code should be reverted. The problem it was
13	solving — conditional routing — is handled instead by the comparator mechanism
14	described here, which works on any box.
15	
16	Similarly, the `branch` box kind (issue 108) is removed in favour of this mechanism.
17	
18	## Current behavior
19	
20	Every box has named output ports. Routing is done either by:
21	- `branch` boxes with named ports and hard-coded predicates, or
22	- `llm-route` boxes with named ports and an Ollama routing call.
23	
24	Both approaches require a dedicated box kind. The connection schema uses
25	`from_port` for these boxes and `from_output` for call boxes — two parallel
26	fields, only one ever set.
27	
28	## Intended behavior
29	
30	Every box has exactly **one output wire** carrying whatever the function
31	returned (raw, as a single value). There are no named output ports.
32	
33	A box may optionally have a **comparator** configured. When a comparator is
34	active, the single output wire splits into three wires: `lt`, `eq`, and `gt`.
35	The executor compares the output value against a literal number. If the output
36	is not a strict number, the executor halts with an error — there is no fallback.
37	
38	The comparator is configured per box via a `comparand` string field (the
39	literal number to compare against) stored in the box file. The inspector shows:
40	- A toggle button labelled **compare** next to the output section.
41	- When active, a text input for the comparand value.
42	
43	Connection schema changes:
44	- Old: `{from_box, from_output|from_port, to_box, to_input}`
45	- New: `{from_box, from_branch, to_box, to_input}`
46	  where `from_branch` is `null` (no comparator, one wire) or `"lt"`/`"eq"`/`"gt"`.
47	
48	The canvas renders one output dot per box by default. When a comparator is
49	active, it renders three stacked dots labelled lt / eq / gt.
50	
51	## Suggested implementation steps
52	
53	1. **Box schema** — add optional `comparand` string to the box file format.
54	   Remove `outputs` array from call box schema. Remove `ports` array and
55	   predicate fields.
56	
57	2. **Connection schema** — replace `from_output`/`from_port` with `from_branch`
58	   (`null` or `"lt"`/`"eq"`/`"gt"`). Update `src/001-schema.lua` validation
59	   and `src/003-loader.lua` connection loading.
60	
61	3. **Executor (`src/004-executor.lua`)**:
62	   - Remove `branch` and `llm-route` kind handling from the execute loop.
63	   - Remove `fire_connections` named-port logic for both kinds.
64	   - After a call box runs: if `box.comparand` is set, parse it as number,
65	     compare against the output value (`lt`/`eq`/`gt`), and fire only the
66	     connection whose `from_branch` matches. If value is not a number, halt
67	     with error. If no comparator, fire the one connection whose `from_branch`
68	     is null.
69	
70	4. **Canvas rendering (`assets/js/002-boxes.js`)** — one output dot per box;
71	   if `box.comparand` is set, render three stacked dots with labels.
72	
73	5. **Wire drawing (`assets/js/006-wires.js`)**:
74	   - Remove `from_port`/`from_output` dual-field logic.
75	   - Use `from_branch` to identify which dot a wire originates from.
76	   - Color lt/eq/gt wires distinctly if desired.
77	
78	6. **Inspector (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`)**:
79	   - Remove `branch` and `llm-route` kind options from dropdown.
80	   - Remove output port list for call boxes.
81	   - Add compare toggle button and comparand input field.
82	   - Input port names are read-only (derived from parsing); only literal values
83	     are editable (see issue 208).
84	
85	7. **File browser (`assets/js/007-filebrowser.js`)** — on function select, set
86	   `box.inputs` from parsed argument names; do NOT set `box.outputs` (no named
87	   outputs).
88	
89	## Related documents

91	- assets/js/002-boxes.js — canvas dot rendering
92	- assets/js/004-inspector.js — compare toggle, comparand field
93	- assets/js/006-wires.js — connection drawing, from_branch field
94	- src/001-schema.lua — box and connection validation
95	- src/003-loader.lua — connection loading
96	- src/004-executor.lua — fire_connections, comparator evaluation
97	- docs/001-architecture.md — box and connection file format
98

1	# 217 — Concat box with per-input variadic ports and auto-grow/shrink
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	No standard concat box exists. No mechanism exists for a box to have a variable
8	number of input wires on a single logical port.
9	
10	## Intended behavior
11	
12	### Part A — text library box
13	`libs/text.lua` exposes two functions:
14	
15	`M.concat(sep, ...)` — join N strings:
16	- `sep` — separator string (e.g. `"\n\n"`)
17	- `...` — any number of text values to join (variadic)
18	- returns a single `result` port
19	
20	The function is variadic so its `text` input can expand to any count without
21	modifying the source file.
22	
23	`M.split(text, sep)` — split one string into parts:
24	- `text` — the input string
25	- `sep` — the separator to split on (plain string, not a pattern)
26	- returns a single `result` port containing a JSON-encoded array of the parts
27	
28	Output ports are named at wire-design time, so a variable number of runtime
29	parts cannot map to separate wires. A JSON array on one port is the only
30	consistent design — the downstream box decodes it.
31	
32	Note: one output wire per box is a deliberate design constraint, not a missing
33	feature. Positional multi-output was explicitly rejected as fragile (multiple
34	return statements with the same tuple width are indistinguishable). The
35	comparator (lt/eq/gt branching) is the only multi-path mechanism. Whatever the
36	function returns goes down the single output wire as one value — arrays or JSON
37	objects if multiple values need to travel together.
38	
39	### Part B — per-input variadic flag
40	
41	Variadic is a property of a specific input port, not the box as a whole. A box
42	could have `sep` (fixed) and `text` (variadic). The inspector shows a toggle on
43	each input to mark it variadic.
44	
45	#### Data model
46	
47	The box JSON gains a `variadic_inputs` set (array of base names):
48	```json
49	{
50	  "inputs": ["sep", "text_0", "text_1", "text_2"],
51	  "variadic_inputs": ["text"]
52	}
53	```
54	
55	Slots of a variadic input are stored as `<base>_<index>` in the `inputs` array.
56	The executor already passes all inputs positionally — no executor changes needed.
57	Connections reference slots by their indexed name (`"text_0"`, `"text_1"`, etc.).
58	
59	The parser (Lua: detects `...`, bash: detects `$@` after shift) can auto-populate
60	`variadic_inputs` when a file is selected via the file browser. For other languages
61	(C, etc.) the user sets the toggle manually in the inspector — the executor contract
62	already supports N positional args via `arg_count`, so C functions reading `argv[]`
63	in a loop work without any changes.
64	
65	#### Auto-grow
66	When a wire is connected to the LAST slot of a variadic input, the editor appends
67	a new empty slot (`text_N+1`) to `box.inputs` and saves the box. The new slot
68	appears immediately as an open port.
69	
70	#### Auto-shrink
71	When a wire is disconnected from any slot of a variadic input:
72	1. Remove that slot from `box.inputs`.
73	2. Rename all subsequent slots down by one (`text_2` → `text_1`, etc.).
74	3. Update every connection that referenced a renamed slot:
75	   - `to_input` in the connection record on this box
76	   - The corresponding `from_output` side on the source box (connections are stored
77	     in both endpoint files; both must be updated atomically).
78	4. Keep at least one slot for the variadic input (never shrink below `text_0`).
79	
80	Middle-port removal is handled by the same rename-and-compact step: remove the cut
81	slot, shift all higher-indexed slots down, update their wires. The user always sees
82	a dense, gap-free list of ports.
83	
84	## Open questions before implementing Part B
85	- Rename atomicity: the server's `PUT /maps/:name/boxes/:id` writes one box at a
86	  time. Updating the connection in the source box requires a second PUT. These are
87	  two separate writes — consider whether a partial failure leaves the map in an
88	  inconsistent state, and whether a `PUT /maps/:name/connections` batch endpoint
89	  is worth adding first.
90	- Should the file browser parser set `variadic_inputs` automatically when it
91	  detects `...` in a Lua signature, and if so, which argument specifically?
92	
93	  -- nah let's just make the user set the variadic property manually. Unless we can put it in the language driver
94	     somehow? but I don't think that's really possible in the design. Thoughts?
95	
96	## Suggested implementation sequence
97	1. Part A: implement `libs/text.lua` with `M.concat(sep, ...)`.
98	2. Part B schema: add `variadic_inputs` to box schema and validator.
99	3. Part B editor: auto-grow on wire connect; auto-shrink + rename on wire disconnect.
100	4. Part B inspector: variadic toggle per input port.
101	5. Part B parser: auto-detect `...` in Lua and set `variadic_inputs`.
102	
103	## Relevant files
104	- `libs/ollama.lua` — reference pattern for a library box
105	- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — wire connect/disconnect events
106	- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — input port list, toggle rendering
107	- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator (`variadic_inputs` field)
108	- `src/005-http-server.lua` — PUT box endpoint (rename propagation)
109	- `issues/208-port-literal-values.md` — `sep` will likely use literal port values
110	
```

1	# 219 — Map compiler: generate standalone source code from a box graph
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	The soramech-runner interprets the box graph at runtime. To execute a map, the
8	user must have SoraMech installed. The runner shells out to a language driver for
9	each box, captures stdout, and routes values to the next box. The runtime
10	dependency on SoraMech and the stdout-as-IPC design are both fragile.
11	
12	## Intended behavior
13	The editor compiles a map into a standalone source file (or script) that runs
14	without SoraMech. The box graph is an authoring artifact — the output of the
15	editor is a real program.
16	
17	### What the compiler produces
18	
19	**Pure Lua map** → a single `.lua` file that requires each box's source file
20	and chains calls directly:
21	```lua
22	local greet = require("src/greet")
23	local write = require("src/write_result")
24	write.write_result(greet.hello())
25	```
26	Runnable with `luajit generated.lua`. No SoraMech, no drivers, no IPC.
27	
28	**Mixed-language map** → a shell script that invokes each box's binary or
29	interpreter in sequence, passing values through named temp files rather than
30	stdout. Each step reads its input from a file and writes its output to a file.
31	The script is self-contained and inspectable.
32	
33	**Comparator (branch) nodes** → if/elseif chains in the generated code.
34	
35	### What stays in the box JSON
36	Canvas positions, labels, wire layout — everything the editor needs to display
37	and edit the graph. The JSON is the editor's internal representation. The
38	compiled output is the deliverable.
39	
40	### Why stdout-as-IPC is the wrong model
41	The current runtime pipes each box's return value through stdout. Problems:
42	- A box that prints debug output corrupts the wire value
43	- Shell process overhead per box
44	- Can't pass binary or large values reliably
45	- Values are transient — can't inspect mid-run
46	
47	The compiler eliminates IPC for same-language maps (direct function calls).
48	For mixed-language maps, file-based IPC is used instead of stdout:
49	each wire becomes a named temp file. The generated script writes/reads
50	explicitly. Files persist after the run and can be inspected.
51	
52	### Language runner libraries (alternative to the current driver model)
53	For multi-language support without a runtime, each language needs a small
54	shim that:
55	- reads its input value from a file path passed as argv
56	- calls the box function
57	- writes the output value to a file path passed as argv
58	
59	The compiler generates calls to these shims. The shims are minimal (~30 lines)
60	and are the only per-language artifact needed. No driver contract, no stdout,
61	no JSON array wrapping. A new language requires only a new shim, not a new
62	driver script with a parsing contract.
63	
64	### The canvas/connection relationship
65	The box JSON currently stores connections in both endpoint files. The compiler
66	reads these to determine call order (topological sort). Once compiled, the
67	connections are embedded in the generated code — the JSON is not needed at
68	runtime. If someone reads the generated code, they can see exactly which
69	functions call which, without needing the JSON.
70	
71	## Design constraints
72	- The editor has no conception of running maps. It creates and edits box graphs.
73	  The compiler is a separate CLI tool invoked outside the editor.
74	- The compiler writes its output into `maps/:name/output/run.lua` (pure Lua) or
75	  `maps/:name/output/run.sh` (mixed). The user invokes this directly.
76	- No "compile" button in the editor. No "run" button in the editor.
77	
78	## Open questions
79	- Primary target language: Lua first, shell script fallback for mixed maps?
80	- For Lua↔C wires: emit LuaJIT FFI calls (C compiled to `.so`) or persistent
81	  subprocess? FFI is faster; subprocess is simpler to generate.
82	- For Lua↔Bash wires: persistent subprocess + anonymous pipe (one spawn per
83	  bash runtime at program start, reused across all calls).
84	- Are runner shims checked into the map's `src/` or shipped globally?
85	- Should the compiler use `shm_open` shared memory for cross-language wire
86	  values, or persistent subprocess + pipe? Shared memory is language-agnostic
87	  and faster; pipe is simpler and works without FFI.
88	
89	## Suggested implementation sequence
90	1. Write the topological sort: given a box graph, produce a linear execution
91	   order respecting dependency edges. (Executor queue logic is the reference.)
92	2. Write a Lua code emitter: for a pure-Lua map, emit `require` calls and
93	   chained function calls in topo order, handling comparator branches as
94	   if/elseif in the generated file.
95	3. Write a CLI entry point: `soramech-compile.lua <map-dir>` that loads the
96	   graph, runs the emitter, and writes `output/run.lua`.
97	4. For mixed maps: choose IPC mechanism (FFI, shm, or persistent subprocess)
98	   and emit the appropriate glue in the generated script.
99	
100	## Relevant files
101	- `src/004-executor.lua` — topological sort and execution model to adapt
102	- `src/003-loader.lua` — box graph loading, connection traversal
103	- `docs/001-architecture.md` — needs update once compiler exists
104	- `issues/completed/102-language-driver-interface.md` — driver model reference
105	
```

7	The editor has no mechanism to trigger compilation of a map. Maps are only

23	### Compiled artifacts: assets directory
24	When compilation is eventually wired in, pressing the button triggers a
25	build that produces a self-contained output directory alongside the map:
26	
27	```

29	    pool-runner          ← the compiled C entry point (008-pool-runner.c)

31	    bin/                 ← compiled per-box binaries (C boxes → .so or binary)

34	
35	The compiled directory is the map's deployment artifact. Running
36	`maps/<map-name>/compiled/pool-runner` executes the map using the thread
37	pool executor, with no dependency on the editor or the Lua interpreter path.
38	
39	The `src/` copy inside `compiled/` is what the pool runner references at

44	The compile step does not treat any language as special. Each box's language
45	determines which invocation wrapper is selected at compile time. The same

47	the language at the top level. The per-language wrapper spec (issue 303) is
48	what parameterizes the build for each box.

None of the three knows about the others\nat runtime.\n\n```\n  Browser (assets/index.html)\n       |  HTTP (file CRUD)\n       v\n  src/006-server-main.lua       [map directory]\n                                maps/<name>/\n                                  meta.json\n                                  boxes/\n                                  data/\n                                  src/\n                                  compiled/   (after compile button)\n                                  tmp/ -> /tmp/<name>/\n       ^\n       | reads & writes\n  Runner (one of):\n    src/007-runner-main.lua     ← phase 2, synchronous Lua interpreter\n    soramech-pool (binary)      ← phase 3, C thread pool runner\n```\n\n### src/006-server-main.lua (the editor's HTTP backend)\n\nThin file CRUD proxy. Receives JSON requests from the browser and\ntranslates them into reads and writes on the map directory. No logic\nbeyond path validation and basic consistency checks (e.g. reject a\ndelete if the box is still referenced by another box's connection\nlist).\n\nStarted with: `luajit src/006-server-main.lua [port]` (default 7700).\nThe `run` script at the project root starts the server and opens the\neditor.\n\nThe editor is editor-only — no run button, no run results display.\nThe runner is invoked separately, by command line. `last-run.jsonl`\n(issue 311) is the runner's output, consumed by external tooling, not\nby the editor.\n\n### Phase 2 runner — `src/007-runner-main.lua`\n\nSynchronous Lua interpreter. Loads a map directory, validates the\ngraph, walks boxes in dependency order, invokes language drivers per\nbox (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/c.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`). Each box\ninvocation is wrapped in a `task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` boundary that\nmatches the phase 3 thread pool's action signature.\n\nThis is the development target while the editor is being built out.\n\n### Phase 3 runner — `soramech-pool` (planned, issues 301–311)\n\nC binary that owns a 3d-rts thread pool. Each box invocation is a\npool task; worker threads run them concurrently. Language code is\ncalled through **language specs** (issue 303), shared libraries\n(`langs/<name>/spec.so`) loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Lua and C\nspecs are in-process; the Bash spec talks to a persistent subprocess\nover a Unix domain socket. Wire values live in **slots** in process\nheap memory (issue 302) — fixed-size with reference counting, plus a\nlarge-value heap for variable-size payloads.\n\nPhase 3 replaces the phase 2 runner wholesale. The synchronous path\ndoes not survive into phase 3; the editor and the map directory\nformat are unchanged across the cutover.\n\n### assets/index.html (the editor)\n\nStatic HTML + vanilla JS. Infinite-scroll canvas. Box diagram editor.\nTalks to `src/006-server-main.lua` for all file operations. No run\nbutton, no compile button (yet — issue 222 adds a placeholder\n\"Compile\" button as part of phase 2). The runner is invoked\nseparately.\n\n## Map directory format\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n  meta.json          — { name, description, entry_box_id, src_dirs?, lang? }\n  boxes/\n    <id>.json        — one file per box (see Box file format below)\n  data/\n    <name>.json      — Lua table as JSON; sections have \"constant\": bool\n  src/\n    *.lua, *.c, *.sh — box function source files\n  compiled/          — produced by the compile button (issue 222)\n    pool-runner      — the compiled C entry point for this map\n    src/             — copy of every source file the map uses\n    bin/             — compiled .so files (C boxes via the C language spec)\n    manifest.json    — every box, its language, its compiled artifact path\n  tmp/               — symlink to /tmp/<name>/\n    last-run.json    — phase 2 run snapshot (single document)\n    last-run.jsonl   — phase 3 run log (JSON Lines, issue 311)\n    logs/            — additional run logs\n```\n\nNote: the phase 2 `drivers.json` file is gone. Language selection in\nphase 2 is by file extension via the `drivers/` directory; in phase 3\nthe spec registry resolves languages by `box.lang` against\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` — no map-local config file needed.\n\n## Box file format\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"trim\",\n  \"label\": \"Trim whitespace\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\": \"src/strings.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"trim\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"text\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ],\n  \"output_capacity\": 4096,\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"trim\",\n      \"from_branch\": null,\n      \"to_box\": \"next-box-id\",\n      \"to_input\": \"text\"\n    }\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 120, \"y\": 340 }\n}\n```\n\nEvery box has exactly **one output wire**. There is no `outputs`\narray. Whatever the function returns travels down the single output\nwire as one value (issue 218). Multiple values that need to travel\ntogether are encoded as JSON or a struct and decoded downstream.\n\n`output_capacity` declares the maximum number of bytes the slot\nallocator (issue 302) reserves for the output. `0` (or omitted) means\nvariable-size — the slot stores a handle into the large-value heap.\n\n### Comparator boxes\nA box may carry a `comparand` field (a literal number as a string).\nWhen set, the dispatch layer compares the input value to the\ncomparand and fires only the connection whose `from_branch` matches\n`\"lt\"` / `\"eq\"` / `\"gt\"`. Comparators have no `ref` / `fn` — the\nrouting logic lives in the dispatch layer (issue 304). The output\nslot carries the input value through unchanged.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"classify\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"comparand\": \"0\",\n  \"inputs\": [{ \"name\": \"value\", \"type\": \"number\" }],\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"classify\", \"from_branch\": \"lt\", \"to_box\": \"negative\", \"to_input\": \"n\" },\n    { \"from_box\": \"classify\", \"from_branch\": \"eq\", \"to_box\": \"zero\",     \"to_input\": \"n\" },\n    { \"from_box\": \"classify\", \"from_branch\": \"gt\", \"to_box\": \"positive\", \"to_input\": \"n\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nThe earlier `branch` box kind with named ports is removed (see issue\n210). Comparator + `from_branch` is the only branching mechanism.\n\n### Iterator boxes\nA box may carry an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\noutput slot names. The dispatch layer routes the input value to the\nslot named `iterator_outputs[counter]`, advances the counter (mod\nlength), and re-spawns itself to consume the next queued input. No\nfunction is invoked — iterators are pure routing primitives. Issue\n221 covers the model; 213 covers the queued-input semantics.\n\n### Connections\nConnections are written to BOTH endpoint box files. The runner\nvalidates at load time that both ends agree. Disagreement is a hard\nerror.\n\n```json\n{ \"from_box\": \"...\", \"from_branch\": null|\"lt\"|\"eq\"|\"gt\"|\"<iter-slot>\",\n  \"to_box\": \"...\",   \"to_input\": \"...\" }\n```\n\n`from_branch` is `null` for plain call boxes (single output wire).\n\n## Language spec system (phase 3)\n\nEach language is a **spec** — a `.so` library at\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` symbol with\n`init` / `teardown` / `compile` / `invoke` callbacks. The pool runner\nloads every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup via `dlopen`. The spec\ncontract (issue 303) is uniform across languages; no language is\nprivileged.\n\nReference specs ship with SoraMech:\n- `langs/lua/spec.so` — in-process via `lua_State`, no compile step (issue 306)\n- `langs/c/spec.so`   — in-process via `dlopen`, with a compile step that generates a wrapper (issue 307)\n- `langs/bash/spec.so`— out-of-process via Unix domain socket to a persistent subprocess (issue 308)\n\nA user adds a new language (Python, Rust, anything) by writing a new\nspec under `langs/<name>/`. SoraMech itself does not transpile or\nconvert source between languages.\n\nThe phase 2 `drivers/*.sh` scripts retire when phase 3 lands. They\nimplement the same idea (one process per call, stdout as channel)\nthat the spec system replaces with persistent runtimes and\nlength-prefix-framed sockets / direct function pointers.\n\n## Execution model — phase 2 (synchronous)\n\nThe runner walks the graph depth-first from the entry box. Each box\ncall:\n\n1. Collect inputs: read wired output values from predecessor boxes.\n2. Invoke driver: shell out to the appropriate driver script.\n3. Collect output: decode single JSON value from driver stdout.\n4. Store output: held in runner memory, keyed by box id.\n5. Fire connections: enqueue boxes whose input dependencies are now\n   met.\n\nEach step is wrapped in a `task_fn` boundary so the runner can be\nswapped for the phase 3 pool runner without changing the box\nexecution model. Phase 2 is single-threaded.\n\n## Execution model — phase 3 (thread pool)\n\nThe C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool with N worker threads.\nEach box invocation is a task. The dispatch layer (issue 304) is the\nworker-side action: read inputs from slots → invoke the language\nspec (or route, for comparators / iterators) → write output to a\nslot → unref consumed inputs → fire downstream connections.\n\nSlots are per-task ring buffers with reference-counted lifetime\n(issue 302). Wires hold references; producers push, consumers peek\nor pop. The wait list on each slot is the synchronization primitive\nthat parks blocked tasks until a producer fills the slot.\n\nThe pool runner has no embedded Lua. It is C from `main` down to the\nlanguage spec boundary; only inside a Lua spec's `invoke` does Lua\ncode run, and only inside that worker's `lua_State`. The graph\nloader is also pure C (issue 305) — phase 2's\n`src/003-loader.lua` retires.\n\nSee `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` for the full IPC and threading\ndiscussion, including the blocking-semantics constraint on long-\nrunning operations.\n\n## Data files\n\nPersistent data lives in `data/<name>.json`. Format:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"constant\": false,\n  \"fields\": {\n    \"history\": [],\n    \"config\": { \"constant\": true, \"value\": { \"model\": \"soramind-default\" } }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nTop-level `constant: true` makes the whole file read-only.\nIndividual fields can be flagged constant within an otherwise\nmutable file. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.\n\nEphemeral state (scratch tables, run logs, the `last-run.jsonl`\noutput) goes to `tmp/`, a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Survives\nthe run but not a reboot — intentionally.\n",

{
  "content":"# SoraMech — Language Driver System\n\n## Two systems, one filename\n\nPhase 2 used **driver scripts** — shell wrappers under `drivers/`\nthat the synchronous runner invoked one process per box call.\n\nPhase 3 uses **language specs** — `.so` libraries under `langs/`\nloaded by the C pool runner via `dlopen`, with persistent per-worker\nruntimes.\n\nSame idea, different mechanism. Phase 3 replaces phase 2 wholesale\nwhen it lands. This document covers both, since the project lives in\nphase 2 today and the phase 3 design is fully specified.\n\n## Phase 2 — Driver scripts (current)\n\nA driver is a shell script. It knows how to invoke a function in one\nlanguage. The synchronous runner looks up the file extension, finds\nthe driver script, and calls it.\n\n### Driver contract\n\nThe runner invokes a driver as:\n\n```\n<driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [<arg> ...]\n```\n\nArguments are always strings. Structured values (tables, arrays) are\npassed as JSON strings and decoded by the driver.\n\nThe driver must:\n- Exit 0 on success, nonzero on failure\n- Print one JSON value to stdout — string, number, boolean, object,\n  or null. One output wire per box.\n- Print error messages to stderr on failure\n\nMulti-output tuple returns are not supported. Each box has exactly\none output wire (issue 218).\n\n### Built-in driver scripts\n\nShipped in the project's `drivers/` directory:\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — invokes a Lua function via `luajit`\n- `drivers/c.sh` — compiles `.c` (mtime cache) and runs the binary\n- `drivers/bash.sh` — sources the `.sh` and calls the function\n\nUser-added drivers go in the same directory and are picked up by\nextension.\n\n### What's wrong with this model\n\nProcess spawn cost dominates each call (1–10 ms per language).\nStdout is a fragile channel — debug prints inside box code corrupt\nthe wire value. Each invocation is its own fresh interpreter; there\nis no persistent runtime between calls. These are the limitations\nphase 3 fixes.\n\n## Phase 3 — Language specs (planned)\n\nEach language is a small C library implementing the spec interface\ndefined in issue 303. The pool runner loads every\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup; the spec interface is uniform\nacross languages, with no privileged language.\n\n### Spec interface\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path,\n                     const box_t *box);\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n                    const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n                    int n_inputs,\n                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity,\n                    int *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n`init` runs once per worker thread at pool startup. `teardown` runs\nat shutdown. `compile` runs at map load time for languages that need\nit (C). `invoke` runs once per box invocation.\n\nThe spec receives input bytes and writes output bytes — never\ninteracts with slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads\ninputs from slots into byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, takes\nback bytes, writes them to the output slot.\n\n### Reference specs\n\n- **Lua** (issue 306) — handle is a `lua_State` per worker. `invoke`\n  loads the box file (cached in the registry), pushes typed\n  arguments, calls via `lua_pcall`, serializes the return value.\n- **C** (issue 307) — handle is a `dlopen`-cache per worker.\n  `compile` generates a wrapper from the box's declared inputs and\n  return type, then runs `cc` to produce the `.so`. `invoke` does\n  `dlsym` and a direct function-pointer call.\n- **Bash** (issue 308) — handle is a Unix domain socket connected\n  to a persistent `bash-server.sh` subprocess. `invoke` sends a\n  framed request, reads a framed response.\n\nThe Lua and C specs are in-process (Option 1 in\n`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`). The Bash spec is out-of-process\n(Option 3) — proof that the spec interface accommodates languages\nthat cannot be embedded.\n\n### Adding a new language\n\nA user adds Python, Rust, or anything else by writing a new spec:\n\n1. Create `langs/<name>/spec.c` implementing the four callbacks.\n2. Create `langs/<name>/Makefile` that builds `spec.so`.\n3. Add the language to `meta.json src_dirs` if necessary so the\n   editor's file browser can see source files.\n\nThe pool runner picks up the new spec at the next startup. No\nSoraMech code change required.\n\nFor full implementation guidance, see the future\n`docs/005-language-specs.md` (referenced from issue 303). For the\nspec contract itself, issue 303.\n\n## Migration: phase 2 → phase 3\n\nWhen phase 3 lands:\n\n| Phase 2                              | Phase 3                              |\n|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `drivers/lua.sh`                     | `langs/lua/spec.so`                  |\n| `drivers/c.sh`                       | `langs/c/spec.so`                    |\n| `drivers/bash.sh`                    | `langs/bash/spec.so`                 |\n| `drivers.json` (per-map)             | (none — spec registry is global)     |\n| stdout as channel                    | direct function call / Unix socket   |\n| One process per call                 | Persistent runtimes                  |\n| Single output wire (JSON-encoded)    | Single output slot (typed bytes)     |\n\nBox JSON does not change shape — `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`\nremain. Phase 3 reads the same files phase 2 reads. The runtime\nmechanism beneath the box is what changes.\n\n## Relevant issues\n\n- 102 (completed) — phase 2 driver interface\n- 218 (completed) — single-output driver contract\n- 303 — phase 3 language spec contract\n- 306 — Lua language spec\n- 307 — C language spec\n- 308 — Bash language spec\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/003-driver-system.md"
}
```

The\n\"compile\" step bridges from \"an editable map directory\" to \"a\nself-contained deployable directory\" that includes the binary, all\nsource files, all compiled `.so`s, and a manifest.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nThe compile step (triggered by the editor's Compile button, issue\n222, or by the CLI) walks a map and produces a `compiled/`\nsubdirectory:\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/compiled/\n    pool-runner          ← the soramech-pool binary, copied here\n    src/                 ← copy of every source file the map uses\n    bin/                 ← per-box compiled .so files (C boxes)\n    langs/               ← copy of language spec .so files needed\n    manifest.json        ← every box, its language, its compiled artifact path\n```\n\nThe `compiled/` directory is the deployment artifact. Running\n`./compiled/pool-runner` executes the map without any reference to\nthe editor, the live `src/` outside `compiled/`, or any external\nSoraMech installation. Ship the directory to someone else and it\nruns.\n\n### What the compile step does\n\n1. **Walk the graph.** Use the same loader logic the runtime uses\n   (issue 305) to enumerate boxes, languages, and source files.\n2. **Copy source.** Every file referenced by `box.ref` is copied\n   into `compiled/src/`. The map's local `src/` is the only place\n   `package.path` searches at runtime (per issue 306), so all\n   dependencies must land here. This includes vendored libraries\n   the user wired in (`libs/json.lua`, `libs/ollama.lua`, etc.).\n3. **Compile per-box artifacts.** For each language present in the\n   map, invoke that spec's `compile` callback (issue 303). The C\n   spec generates a wrapper from the box's declared signature and\n   produces a `.so` in `compiled/bin/` (issue 307). Lua and Bash\n   specs have no compile step; their files are copied verbatim.\n4. **Copy spec libraries.** The `langs/<name>/spec.so` files for\n   every language used in the map are copied to\n   `compiled/langs/<name>/spec.so`. The pool runner discovers\n   specs relative to its binary location, so this co-location is\n   what makes the deployment self-contained.\n5. **Copy the runner binary.** `soramech-pool` is copied to\n   `compiled/pool-runner`. (A symlink works too, for development.)\n6. **Write the manifest.** `compiled/manifest.json` lists every\n   box, its language, the path of its compiled artifact (or source\n   file for interpreted languages), and the SoraMech build version\n   the deployment was compiled against.\n\n### What stays in the box JSON\nCanvas positions, labels, wire layout — everything the editor needs\nto display and edit the graph. The JSON is the editor's\nrepresentation of the graph. The compiled directory is the\ndeliverable. The two never need to be in sync after compile —\nthe compiled output is frozen at compile time.\n\n### Editor invocation (issue 222)\nThe Compile button in the editor triggers the same compile step via\na new server endpoint `POST /maps/<name>/compile`. The server\nshells out to a `soramech-compile` CLI (or invokes the same code\nin-process — implementation detail). Output / errors stream back to\nthe editor for display. The editor itself does not run the\ncompiled output; the user invokes `./compiled/pool-runner` from a\nterminal.\n\nThis supersedes the earlier \"no compile button in the editor\" stance\nin the original issue text — issue 222 is the formal addition of\nthe button.\n\n### CLI invocation\nA standalone CLI tool `soramech-compile <map-dir>` runs the same\npipeline without the server. Useful for CI and headless deployment.\n\n## Design constraints\n\n- The editor still has no conception of *running* maps — only\n  compiling them. Run is a separate concern (the user invokes the\n  pool-runner binary themselves).\n- Compile is incremental: mtime comparison on each artifact. If a\n  source file is newer than its compiled output, re-compile that\n  one. Otherwise skip. (Per the C spec, issue 307.)\n- Errors at any stage abort the compile and surface a precise\n  message (which box, which file, what failed).\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Whether the compiled directory bundles a copy of `soramech-pool`\n  or a symlink. Bundling makes the directory portable across\n  machines; symlinking saves disk on the dev machine. Configurable\n  via a `--portable` flag.\n- Multi-architecture: a compiled directory built on x86_64 won't\n  run on arm64. Out of scope — users compile on the target\n  architecture. Could later add a cross-compile mode if the SoraMind\n  cluster is mixed-arch.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Walk the map graph using the C loader (issue 305) — the same\n   code the runtime uses. Emit a list of (box, language, files).\n2. Implement the source-copy step. Every `box.ref` file plus any\n   `require`/`source`/`#include` dependencies (resolvable via\n   static analysis or just-copy-the-whole-libs/-directory).\n3. For C boxes: invoke the C spec's `compile` callback (issue 307)\n   per box. Outputs land in `compiled/bin/`.\n4. Copy `langs/<name>/spec.so` for every language present.\n5. Copy or symlink `soramech-pool`.\n6. Write `manifest.json`.\n7. Wire `POST /maps/<name>/compile` in the server (issue 222\n   button calls this).\n8. Smoke test: compile `maps/hello`, run\n   `./maps/hello/compiled/pool-runner`, verify result matches\n   the phase 2 run.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — the runner binary that gets copied in\n- `langs/<name>/spec.so` — language specs that get copied in\n- `langs/<name>/spec.c::compile` — per-language compile callback\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — UI button\n  that triggers this\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `compile` interface\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — graph-walk logic shared with\n  the runtime\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — C wrapper generation\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — describes the `compiled/` directory\n  layout\n- `issues/completed/102-language-driver-interface.md` — phase 2\n  driver model (historical reference)\n",

1	# 213 — Queued inputs and synchronous task model
2	
3	## Status
4	
5	open
6	
7	## Current behavior
8	
9	Each input port in the executor store holds exactly one value. When an upstream
10	box fires a connection, it overwrites whatever was previously in that slot. A box
11	only runs once (the `visited` guard prevents re-execution). This means:
12	
13	- A box with two upstream feeders only processes the last-arriving value.
14	- Fan-in patterns (many outputs converging on one input) silently drop values.
15	- There is no way to process a stream of values through a box.
16	
17	## Intended behavior
18	
19	Each input port has a **queue** (ordered list) of waiting values instead of a
20	single slot. A box becomes "ready" when all of its required input ports have at
21	least one value in their queue. When a box runs, it pops one value from the
22	front of each required input queue, then runs the task with those values. After
23	the task completes, the box is checked again — if all required queues are still
24	non-empty, it runs again immediately, consuming the next set of inputs.
25	
26	Optional ports (marked with `"optional": true` in the input object) do not gate
27	readiness. If a value is present in an optional port's queue when the task runs,
28	it is consumed; otherwise the task receives nil for that port.
29	
30	This model enables:
31	- Fan-in: A collects 10 values, B collects 1. Each new value to B creates one
32	  task that consumes one A-value and the new B-value.
33	- Pipelines: output of one box feeds into the next, which re-runs for each
34	  arriving value.
35	- Broadcast: one box fans out to two boxes, both of which process that one value.
36	
37	The executor stays **synchronous** in this phase. Coroutines are not required
38	for the synchronous model — the simple approach is: after each box run, re-check
39	all boxes (not just directly connected ones) for readiness and enqueue any that
40	are ready. Run until the queue is empty or an error occurs.
41	
42	## Data model changes
43	
44	**Store**: `store["box_id.port_name"]` changes from a single value to an array
45	of values (a queue). All reads pop from the front; all writes push to the back.
46	
47	**Inputs satisfied**: `inputs_satisfied(box, store)` — a port is satisfied when
48	`#store[key] > 0`. Optional ports are always considered satisfied.
49	
50	**Collect inputs**: `collect_inputs(box, store)` — shifts (pops front) one value
51	from each port's queue and returns the map of port-name → value.
52	
53	**Visited guard**: remove the `visited` flag. Instead, enqueue a box whenever its
54	inputs become satisfied (even if it has run before). This is safe because
55	satisfaction requires queue entries, and collect_inputs consumes them.
56	
57	**Literal values**: pre-seeded literal values are still pushed once into the
58	queue at startup. They are consumed on first run. A wire can push additional
59	values on top of the literal.
60	
61	## Optional port convention
62	
63	In the box file:
64	```json
65	{ "name": "temperature", "type": "any", "optional": true, "value": "0.7" }
66	```
67	
68	`optional: true` means this port does not block readiness. The literal `value`
69	(if present) is still pre-seeded into the queue as a default. Wires can push
70	additional values.
71	
72	## Suggested implementation steps
73	
74	1. **`src/004-executor.lua`** — change store values to arrays. Update
75	   `inputs_satisfied` (check array length, skip optional ports). Update
76	   `collect_inputs` (table.remove from front). Remove `visited` table.
77	   After each `fire_connections`, re-scan all boxes for satisfaction and
78	   enqueue the newly ready ones.
79	
80	2. **`src/001-schema.lua`** — add optional `"optional"` boolean to port objects.
81	
82	3. **`src/004-executor.lua`** — pre-seeding: push literal values into arrays
83	   (`store[key] = { parsed_val }`) instead of assigning directly.
84	
85	4. **`assets/js/004-inspector.js`** — add an "optional" checkbox per input port
86	   row. On change, update `port.optional` and save.
87	
88	## Future: thread pool
89	
90	When the synchronous model is replaced by a thread pool, the queue-per-port
91	design maps directly: a worker thread pops one value from each input queue,
92	runs the task, and pushes outputs to the connected ports' queues. The
93	satisfaction check becomes a condition variable or semaphore per port. The
94	synchronous executor described here is the reference implementation.
95	
96	## Related documents
97	
98	- src/004-executor.lua — execute, inputs_satisfied, collect_inputs, fire_connections
99	- src/001-schema.lua — port schema, optional field
100	- assets/js/004-inspector.js — optional port checkbox
101	- docs/001-architecture.md — store model, box.inputs schema
102	
```

297	A future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`
298	that loads each library into its own isolated "namespace," giving
299	each worker its own copy of the library's symbols (statics
300	included). Two threads using two different namespaces would not
301	share static state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only), so
302	not the default — flagged here as the escape hatch if static-
303	variable races become a real problem.
304	
305	## Build
306	
307	```
308	langs/c/
309	    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation
```

=== 202 ===
# 202 — Fit-to-view on map load

## Status

open

## Blockers

- 201 (boxes must render before fit-to-view can be tested)

## Current behavior

When a map loads, the camera stays at its default position (origin, zoom 1).
If boxes were placed at coordinates far from (0,0), they are off-screen and
the user has no way to know where to look.

## Intended behavior

After `load_map()` completes, the camera is moved and zoomed so that all
loaded boxes are visible with a small margin. If the map is empty, the camera
resets to the origin.

## Suggested implementation steps

1. In `005-app.js`, after populating `Boxes.boxes`, compute the bounding box
   of all box positions (using `box.ui.x`, `box.ui.y`, and `Boxes.box_height`).
2. Compute the center of the bounding box and set `cam.x` / `cam.y` to center
   it in the canvas.
3. Compute zoom so the bounding box fits within the canvas with ~60px margin
   on each side. Clamp zoom to [0.25, 1.5].
4. Call `Canvas.mark_dirty()`.
5. Expose a `fit_to_view()` function from App and wire it to a toolbar button
   so the user can re-center at any time.

## Related documents

- assets/js/001-canvas.js — cam, mark_dirty
- assets/js/002-boxes.js — box_height, BOX_W
- assets/js/005-app.js — load_map

# 203 — Map picker panel

## Status

open

## Current behavior

On first load, the editor shows a browser `prompt()` asking for a server URL
and map name. These are stored in localStorage. The only way to switch maps
is to click "switch map", which clears localStorage and reloads — prompting
again with bare text inputs.

This is friction every time you want to work on a different map.

## Intended behavior

On load, if no server URL or map name is stored, show a proper panel (not a
browser prompt) with:
- A text input for the server URL (default: http://localhost:7700)
- A list of available maps fetched from GET /maps on the server
- Clicking a map name connects to it and loads the editor

The "switch map" button opens this panel again without clearing all of
localStorage (so the server URL is remembered).

The panel should be rendered in the sidebar, replacing the inspector content
while open. Once a map is selected, the normal editor state resumes.

## Suggested implementation steps

1. On `DOMContentLoaded`, if `soramech_map` is not in localStorage, show the
   picker panel instead of loading immediately.
2. The picker panel: server URL text input + "connect" button. On connect,
   call `API.list_maps()` and render a clickable list of map names.
3. On map name click: store URL + name in localStorage, call `API.init()`,
   close the picker, call `load_map()`.
4. "switch map" button opens the picker panel without wiping the server URL.
5. If the server is unreachable, show an error in the panel with a retry
   option.

## Related documents

- assets/js/003-api.js — list_maps()
- assets/js/005-app.js — init(), load_map()
- assets/index.html — sidebar and inspector panel

## Intended behavior

The canvas shows a short hint overlay when the map is empty or when nothing

# 206 — Entry box designation

## Status

open

## Current behavior

The entry box is set in `meta.json` (`entry_box_id` field), but the editor
has no way to show which box is the entry point or to change it. The user
must edit meta.json directly (via the server API or a text editor) to set or
change the entry box.

## Intended behavior

The entry box is visually distinct on the canvas — a small marker or badge
(e.g. a filled triangle or "▶" label) drawn in the top-left corner of the
box header.

Any box can be designated as the entry box from the inspector. When a box is
selected, a "set as entry" button appears at the top of the inspector panel.
Clicking it updates `meta.json` via PUT /maps/:name/meta and redraws the
canvas.

Only one box can be the entry at a time. Changing the entry box immediately
updates the visual marker on the canvas.

## Suggested implementation steps

1. In `005-app.js` `load_map()`, also fetch `meta.json` and store
   `App.meta` (or a module-level variable) with the current entry_box_id.
2. In `002-boxes.js` `draw_box()`, if `box.id === entry_box_id`, draw a
   small "▶" badge in the header area (e.g., left of the label, in the
   accent color for the box kind).
3. In `004-inspector.js` `show()`, add a "set as entry" button at the top
   of the inspector. On click: update the local entry_box_id, call
   `API.put_meta({...meta, entry_box_id: box.id})`, mark canvas dirty.
4. Pass `entry_box_id` into `draw_all` so the renderer knows which box to
   mark.
