1	# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	Wire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values
8	have no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language
9	accessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.
10	
11	## Concept
12	
13	### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks
14	
15	Each box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph
16	loads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing
17	declaration: "the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value
18	into this consumer's named input slot." The producer never owns a
19	slot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.
20	
21	When a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into
22	every downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N
23	pushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into
24	the same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same
25	push-into-input-slot mechanic.
26	
27	Slots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker
28	thread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs
29	(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot
30	addresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not
31	shared memory.
32	
33	### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable
34	
35	A **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's
36	input slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every
37	downstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're
38	just stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the
39	dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot
40	holds at least one value).
41	
42	The **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any
43	counter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so
44	on. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and
45	go.
46	
47	This is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N
48	times where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply
49	(possibly 1, possibly thousands). The difference is just what the
50	task does:
51	- **Plain call task**: invoke spec on the popped values, push the
52	  return to outputs.
53	- **Iterator task**: read box's counter, route the popped value to
54	  output port `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.
55	  No spec invocation.
56	- **Comparator task**: invoke spec on the popped values, compare
57	  the return against `comparand`, route to the matching `lt` /
58	  `eq` / `gt` branch.
59	
60	### All slots are ring buffers
61	
62	There is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,
63	each of `cell_capacity` bytes. Every input port has a ring buffer
64	of compile-time-determined size:
65	
66	- **Default size**: enough cells to absorb the maximum number of
67	  pushes that can happen before the box can drain. For a port fed
68	  by a single non-iterator producer, that's 1. For a port fed by
69	  an iterator, it's the iterator's worst-case backlog (statically
70	  inferred or capped at a high default like 64 with growth).
71	- **Upper bound**: lists grow if backlog exceeds the pre-allocated
72	  size, so n_cells isn't a hard cap on correctness — only on
73	  pre-allocation efficiency.
74	
75	The producer pushes one cell per fan-out path; the consumer pops
76	one cell per invocation. Fan-in is multiple producers pushing into
77	the same input slot in arrival order; the consumer pops in FIFO
78	order.
79	
80	### Asynchrony
81	The store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and
82	freed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization
83	is per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.
84	
85	## Slot layout
86	
87	Each slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`
88	bytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:
89	
90	```
91	Slot header
92	Offset  Size  Field
93	------  ----  -----
94	0       4     refcount        (atomic int32; lifetime counter)
95	4       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)
96	8       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation; 1 for single-value)
97	12      4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)
98	16      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)
99	20      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)
100	21      3     _pad
101	24      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))
102	```
103	
104	Each cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`
105	bytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across
106	slots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing
107	sizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows
108	how big it needs the cells.
109	
110	`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation
111	(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`
112	spins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —
113	if contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without
114	changing the API.
115	
116	Writes to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is
117	advanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to
118	see the complete value at the head cell.
119	
120	## Lifetime and end-of-stream
121	
122	Slots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live
123	from graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference
124	counting — the slot is freed when the run ends, alongside its
125	owning box.
126	
127	### End-of-stream detection (replacing producer refcounts)
128	
129	Each slot tracks the set of upstream producer boxes that may still
130	push into it. When a producer's "no more pushes" condition fires
131	— either it has finished all its invocations, or it transitively
132	depends only on producers that have finished — the dispatch layer
133	removes that producer from the slot's producer set.
134	
135	When the producer set is empty AND the slot's queue is drained,
136	the consumer box has reached end-of-stream on that port. For an
137	iterator, this is what tells the iterator to stop re-spawning. For
138	a non-iterator, this means no further invocations are coming;
139	combined with the same condition on its other input ports, the
140	box itself is done.
141	
142	This replaces the per-slot refcount machinery. The "are upstreams
143	still alive" check is done at the producer-set level, which is
144	cheaper and avoids the contention of refcount churn on hot paths.
145	
146	### Wait list
147	Each slot also owns a wait list — pointers to tasks parked on the
148	slot waiting for a value. When a producer pushes, the slot walks the
149	wait list and tells the pool to re-run those tasks. The wait list is
150	attached to the slot, not to the producer or the consumer.
151	
152	## Backing store
153	
154	Slots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a
155	per-run allocator (described under "Allocation strategy" below) that
156	hands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is
157	sufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write
158	it, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.
159	
160	Synchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for
161	header mutations and a per-slot wait list (above) for blocked tasks.
162	There is no allocator-wide mutex on the read/write path; only the
163	per-size-class free lists in the allocator have their own locks.
164	
165	## Slot creation
166	
167	Slot creation happens at **graph load**, not per task. The graph
168	loader walks every box, allocates one ring buffer per input port,
169	and parks the slot on the box's per-port slot table. The dispatch
170	layer never allocates new slots at runtime in the steady state —
```

Walkthrough of the design as it stands. Let me go layer by layer.

## 1. The big picture

SoraMech is split into three programs:
- **Editor** (web, JS): visual graph editor that writes `maps/<name>/` directory contents.
- **Runner** (C, phase 3): pool runner that executes a map.
- **Server** (Lua, phase 2 → eventually disposable): file CRUD between editor and disk.

The map directory is the contract between editor and runner. Boxes live in `maps/<name>/boxes/*.json`; source files in `maps/<name>/src/`; meta in `maps/<name>/meta.json`. The editor writes and the runner reads.

## 2. The graph

A **box** is a node. Two kinds:
- `call`: invokes a user-written function in some language.
- `data`: language-agnostic file source / sink (issue 229, planned — currently behaves like a colored call box).

A **port** is an input or output position on a box. Inputs are named (from the parsed function signature). Outputs are either a single unnamed port, or three named branches `lt`/`eq`/`gt` (comparator), or N user-named slots (iterator).

A **wire** is a routing declaration: producer's named output port → consumer's named input port. Wires don't own data; they're metadata in the graph.

Three **box modes**, all set per-box rather than per-kind:
- **Plain call**: function runs, returns one value, value goes to all wired downstream consumers unconditionally.
- **Comparator**: same, plus the value is compared to the box's `comparand` field; only the matching branch fires.
- **Iterator**: no function. Per invocation, the box copies its input to one of N output ports based on a counter, then increments. Pure routing.

## 3. Startup (issue 301)

The pool runner's `main`:
1. Parse map path from argv.
2. Load + validate the graph (C loader, issue 305 — replaces phase 2's `003-loader.lua`).
3. For each box: allocate one ring-buffer slot per input port. Sizes from compile-time analysis (1 for non-iterator-fed, larger for iterator-fed, growable on demand).
4. Build per-box runtime state: `box_runtime_state[box_id]` holding the input slot table, the iterator counter (0), the producer set per slot (boxes that may still push there).
5. Create the worker pool (3d-rts vendored library, `libs/task-pool/`). Each worker calls each language spec's `init(worker_idx)` to stand up its per-thread state — one `lua_State`, one persistent Bash subprocess, one C dlopen table per worker.
6. Push every input port's literal value (if set) directly into its slot.
7. For each box whose input set is now satisfied (every input slot has a value), spawn a `dispatch_task_t` and submit to the pool.
8. Main thread sleeps on a condition variable waiting for the active-task counter to hit zero.
9. On wake, write `last-run.jsonl`, tear down workers, exit.

After step 8, **no main-thread orchestration**. Workers drive everything.

## 4. Slots (issue 302, revised)

Each box owns one ring-buffer slot per input port. Slot header is 20 bytes:

```
cell_capacity (4) | n_cells (4) | head (4) | tail (4) | touched (1) | _pad (3)
followed by n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes) of cell data
```

Pushes write a cell + advance `tail`; pops read at `head` + advance `head`. `touched` is a per-slot spinlock byte.

**Allocation strategy**: size-class free lists. Compile time enumerates every distinct slot size; lists pre-populate at startup; allocations are list pops (O(1)). Variable-size payloads (LLM responses, dynamic arrays) live in a separate **large-value heap**; the slot stores a `{size, offset}` handle into it. When a slot's pre-allocated `n_cells` proves too small, the slot grows (lists grow during the run).

**Lifetime**: durable for the run. No per-slot refcounting. End-of-stream is detected via the **producer set** per slot: the dispatch layer tracks which producer boxes may still push, and removes producers as they finish. When the set is empty AND the slot is drained, the consumer has end-of-stream on that port.

## 5. Dispatch (issue 304, revised)

A **task** is `{ box_id, counter }`. That's it. Slots aren't on the task because they're durable on the box.

**Spawning rule** (the synchronization primitive of the whole system):
> When a push to box B's input slot completes, check: does every input slot on B now hold at least one value? If yes, allocate a task with `box_id=B, counter=B.counter`, submit to the pool.

**The dispatch action** (`dispatch_action(task)`), runs on whichever worker pulled the task:

1. **Read inputs**: `slot_pop` from each of B's input slots into heap buffers. Pop drains; values queued behind move forward.
2. **Branch on box mode**:
   - Plain call → invoke spec, write return to outputs.
   - Comparator → invoke spec, write return to outputs, compare return to `comparand`, fire only matching branch.
   - Iterator → no spec, route popped value to `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.
3. **Push to downstream input slots**: the box's connection list has the wire targets. For each wire that should fire (per mode), `slot_push(downstream_input_slot, bytes, size)`. After each push, run the spawn-rule check for that downstream box — possibly spawn another task.
4. **End-of-stream propagation**: if this push was the producer's last expected push, remove this producer from each pushed-to slot's producer set. Empty set + drained queue = consumer's end-of-stream on that port.
5. Return ACT_DONE. Pool decrements active-task counter. If counter hits zero, signal main thread.

No phase blocks. No wait lists. Tasks are spawn-then-run-to-completion.

**Cross-iterator pairing**: when a non-iterator C has two upstream iterators A and B, each port has its own queue, FIFO pop pairs `(A_i, B_i)` deterministically iff A and B push in deterministic order. Concurrent pushes from different workers risk race. Phase 3 ships FIFO; per-invocation index tags are a follow-on if a workload needs strict pairing.

## 6. Language specs (issue 303 + 312)

Each language ships `langs/<name>/spec.so` and `langs/<name>/lexer.js` and `langs/<name>/parser.js` (issue 231, planned).

Spec interface (with the 312 fast-path additions):

```c
typedef struct {
    const char *name, *file_ext;

    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);
    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);
    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path, const box_t *box);

    int   (*invoke_json)  (handle, file, fn, in_data[], in_sizes[], n, out_buf, out_cap, out_size);
    int   (*invoke_native)(handle, file, fn, in_data[], in_sizes[], n, out_buf, out_cap, out_size);

    int   (*native_to_json)(src, src_size, dst, dst_cap, dst_size);
    int   (*json_to_native)(src, src_size, dst, dst_cap, dst_size);
} lang_spec_t;
```

The pool runner `dlopen`s every `langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup and indexes by name and extension.

**Wire format** is JSON by default — every spec implements `invoke_json` for cross-language hops. Same-language wires use `invoke_native` with a per-language native serialization (Lua tables via msgpack or `lua_dump`; C structs via memcpy; Bash strings as-is). The compile step (issue 309) classifies each wire as `fast_path: true | false` based on whether endpoints share a language, and tags the producer's output_format. Dispatch action's input-read branches on this flag — no runtime negotiation.

**Type-annotated cross-language encodings** (primitives as raw bytes, strings length-prefixed, structures as JSON) — open question per 312's implementation note. Decision deferred to implementation start.

**Per-language specs**:
- Lua (306): `lua_State` per worker, file caching via Lua registry, in-process invocation.
- C (307): `dlopen`/`dlsym` per worker, compile callback generates a per-box wrapper that takes a count + pointer array and forwards to the user function.
- Bash (308): persistent subprocess per worker, length-prefixed message protocol over Unix domain socket. Out-of-process because Bash has no embeddable runtime.

## 7. Build / compile (issue 309)

Top-level Makefile orchestrates. Targets:
- `runner` → `soramech-pool` binary, statically linking the pool, slot store, graph loader, dispatch, spec registry.
- `specs` → recurses into each `langs/<name>/Makefile` to build `spec.so`.
- `clean`, `test`, `DEBUG=1`, `STRICT=1` modes.

**Compile-and-package step** (folded in from issue 219, closed): turns an editable map directory into `maps/<name>/compiled/` with the runner binary, source files, per-box `.so`s, language spec `.so`s, and a manifest. Triggered by the editor's Compile button (issue 222) via a `POST /maps/<name>/compile` endpoint and by a CLI `soramech-compile <map-dir>`.

**Compile-time validations** (also during compile):
- Required-input rule (issue 230): every input port has a wire, a literal, or `optional: true`. Compile fails loudly if not.
- Wire fast-path classification (issue 312): each wire tagged `fast_path` per same/different language pair.
- Producer-set determination per input slot for end-of-stream tracking.
- Output sizes per box for the slot-store size-class allocator.

## 8. Quiescence and run output

Each task spawn increments the active-task counter; each ACT_DONE decrements. When the counter hits zero, no task is running and no further spawns are pending — run is over. Iterators that hit end-of-stream stop spawning successors naturally; the counter drains.

**No deadlock concern** at runtime. The graph loader rejects non-iterator cycles and inputs without producers at load time. Spec errors abort the program (no halfway-complete state). Iterator-parked-on-empty-input is the natural EOS condition, not a deadlock.

`last-run.jsonl` is written at the end (issue 311): one JSON line per box invocation with timing, inputs, outputs, errors. Replay-friendly format.

## 9. Cross-cutting concerns

- **No null from missing inputs** (issue 230): compile fails on unwired non-optional ports; absent ≠ explicit null at the spec boundary.
- **Variadic** (per-box flag, issue 217 complete; issue 231 planned for per-language parser): user-tagged in editor, dispatch flattens slots into ordered arg list, language's native variadic syntax handles it.
- **Self-loop wires** (issue 228 complete): allowed; dispatch just pushes from a box's output to its own input slot like any other push.
- **Optional inputs** (issue 230): port's `optional: true` flag; spawn rule allows the task even with that slot empty; the spec's invocation passes a shorter arg list.

## 10. Editor surface to runtime

Things in the editor that produce runtime state:
- `kind`, `ref`, `fn` → which box, which language, which function.
- `inputs[].name`, `inputs[].value`, `inputs[].optional` → input port names, literals, optionality.
- `comparand` → comparator threshold.
- `iterator_outputs[]` → iterator branch names + count.
- `variadic_inputs[]` → which input names are variadic group bases.
- `connections[]` → wires.
- `has_output` → sink box flag.

The runtime never reads anything outside this set from the box JSON. The editor is the source of truth for graph shape; the runner is the source of truth for execution.

---

That's the design end-to-end. Where do you want to dig deeper, or what doesn't sit right?

Good catches — several of these point at design holes. Let me work through them, then we update the issues.

## 1. Why iterator-fed ports get larger buffers

It's backlog absorption. A non-iterator producer pushes its slot **once** for its lifetime; one cell is enough. An iterator produces N values across N invocations; if N is 50 and the consumer can only drain at half the producer's rate, the slot has to hold up to 25 unconsumed values at any moment.

For non-iterator-fed ports, the producer-rate question doesn't arise — there's only ever one push.

## 2. Owning the thread pool, not vendoring 3d-rts

Agreed. The pool is part of SoraMech's surface area; we want full control over the spawn primitive, the worker-context model, and any extensions (tying iterators to specific workers, see §8 below). We'll write a SoraMech-specific pool and refer to 3d-rts only as the design reference / inspiration. Worth updating issue 301.

## 3. Init synchronization

Right — we need a barrier after every worker has called every spec's `init` and before any task is submitted. Otherwise the main thread could push tasks while a worker is still bringing up its `lua_State`, and a task that lands on the not-yet-initialized worker would read a null handle.

The shape: pool startup is a join point. Workers come up, each one runs all the spec inits in some defined order, and signals readiness on a counter. Main thread waits until all N workers have signaled, **then** pushes literals and spawns initial tasks. Worth updating 301.

## 4. The literal re-push problem (you found a real hole)

Right. With the pop-draining model I wrote, a literal pushed once at startup gets consumed by the first task and the second task finds an empty slot. Broken for any box that runs more than once.

The fix is to bring back a distinction I'd flattened: **non-iterator-fed slots are peek-not-pop, iterator-fed slots are pop-and-drain**. Original 302 had this; I lost it in the rewrite.

Concretely:
- A 1-cell slot's read mode is **peek**: the value stays after a read, every subsequent task on this box reads the same value.
- An N-cell slot's read mode is **pop**: each read drains one cell, subsequent tasks see the next value.

For the user's question: a literal pushed at startup stays in the slot. If the box runs 50 times because some other input port (iterator-fed, N-cell, drained) supplies 50 values, each of those 50 task instances peeks the literal. The literal isn't re-pushed — it doesn't need to be.

The spawn-rule check becomes: "every input port's slot has at least one value **available**" — which means "non-empty cell" for both kinds, just with different semantics on read.

This deserves an update to 302, both the slot-read section and the spawn-rule section.

## 5. End-of-stream / producer set — you're right, drop it

Your read is exactly right: the producer-set machinery is overengineering. The active-task counter (issue 301) already handles run termination correctly:
- Each task spawn increments.
- Each ACT_DONE decrements.
- When it hits zero with no pending spawns, the run is over.

The producer-set was answering "should this iterator stop expecting more inputs?" — but iterators don't need to ask that question. They just stop getting tasks when their input slot stops getting pushed. The active-task counter naturally drains, the run ends.

I shouldn't have added the producer-set thing. Let me strip it from 302/304. The end-of-stream condition becomes trivial: there is no end-of-stream condition, just an active-task counter reaching zero.

Box JSON has the producer→consumer relationships; runtime doesn't need to mutate that. You're right that mutating-the-graph-at-runtime felt like garbage collection — it was, and the cost wasn't worth it.

## 6. Large value passed C → Lua

Honest answer: **cross-language large values get copied at the boundary, no way around it**.

Lua's string memory is owned by Lua's GC. C-allocated memory has no relationship to Lua's string table. There's no zero-copy path: even Lua's userdata, which can wrap a C pointer, requires Lua code to call back into C to read bytes — defeating the purpose if you're trying to pass it to a Lua function expecting a string.

The flow:
1. C spec produces 4MB string. Writes it to the large-value heap. Slot cell holds `{size: 4MB, offset: ...}`.
2. Lua spec invoked. Receives the 16-byte handle. Follows the offset, finds the bytes in the large-value heap.
3. **Copies** those bytes into a Lua string via `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, 4MB)`. Lua's GC now owns a copy.
4. The user's Lua function gets a normal Lua string.

The 4MB copy is the price of going across the language boundary. Lua's memory model is incompatible with referencing external memory.

Same-language paths can avoid the copy: C → C can pass the handle directly; the consumer's wrapper reads from the same large-value heap with no copy. Lua → Lua can reuse Lua's own table-passing via `lua_dump`/`lua_load` or msgpack. That's what the same-language fast path (issue 312) buys you.

You're right that this is "an impossible optimization" for cross-language. The right move isn't to optimize the cross-language case — it's to design graphs so large values don't cross language boundaries. The same-language merge research issue (313) eventually lets the build system warn about this kind of crossing.

## 7. Counter as invisible input port

Both work. The choice is between:

**A: Per-box counter state** (current 304). Box has `counter` field. Each spawn snapshots `counter` into the task; box's counter increments. Pro: simple, one int per iterator box, no extra slot machinery. Con: special-cases iterator boxes in the runtime.

**B: Counter as a hidden input slot.** Box has a 1-cell slot named `__counter__` (invisible to user). At spawn time, the dispatch layer pops the counter value, runs the action, pushes counter+1 back to the slot. Pro: counter goes through the same machinery as everything else; no special box state. Con: more pushes/pops on the hot path; the slot is conceptually special even if structurally uniform.

I'd lean A for performance; B is more elegant. Worth picking explicitly — let me know which way and I'll lock it in 304.

## 8. Cross-iterator pairing under "phase 3 as designed"

OK, let's commit to a pairing answer.

The race you're worried about: iterator A produces 50 invocations. Task 1 produces value `a0`, task 2 produces `a1`, etc. Tasks could run on different workers in parallel; if task 2 finishes before task 1, the pushes to consumer C's slot arrive in the wrong order.

But — iterator tasks share the **per-box counter** as state. To spawn task 2, the dispatch layer reads the counter, snapshots it, then increments. Two iterator tasks of the same iterator can't really run in parallel anyway: they have a serial dependency through the counter.

The cleanest answer is **iterators are pinned to a single worker**. Each iterator has its tasks executed sequentially on that worker. Push order = invocation order = FIFO arrival at the consumer's slot, deterministic.

Trade-off: an iterator's invocations don't parallelize across workers. Other tasks (downstream consumers, parallel iterators on different workers) absolutely do. Most graphs aren't bottlenecked on a single iterator's throughput; they're bottlenecked on the consumers' work.

For cases where one iterator IS the bottleneck and parallel invocations would help — that's the "indexed pairing" follow-on. Each push tags its value with the iterator's counter snapshot; consumer's slot becomes a priority-insert structure that pops in tag order. Strict ordering, parallel iterator invocations. Complex enough that we don't ship it without proof we need it.

So phase 3 as designed: **single-worker iterators + FIFO consumer slots, deterministic pairing as a free consequence**.

---

## Issue updates this implies

Let me consolidate. I'd update:

1. **301** — replace "vendored 3d-rts" with "SoraMech-owned pool, design referenced from 3d-rts." Add an explicit init-barrier section before task submission begins.
2. **302** — restore the peek-vs-pop distinction (1-cell slots peek, N-cell slots pop). Drop the producer-set section. Update the spawn-rule wording.
3. **304** — drop end-of-stream propagation. Pick between counter-as-box-state vs counter-as-hidden-slot (waiting on your call). Add the iterator-pinned-to-worker rule for deterministic pairing.

Should I make these updates? And which counter model do you want — per-box state, or hidden input slot?

Right, you're correcting valid mistakes in my framing. Let me work through the answers, then make the updates.

## 1. Box vs task clarification

You're right, my terminology was sloppy. To re-state precisely:

**Boxes** are graph nodes — static, defined in JSON, exist for the run. **Tasks** are box invocations — ephemeral, allocated when a spawn fires. A box may have 1 or N tasks during a run.

What I meant by "iterator producer pushes 50 times": *the iterator box, across its 50 task invocations, performs 50 pushes total.* Each individual iterator task does the same single push that any task does. The box is what fires multiple times; each task does exactly one thing.

You're also right that "iterator vs non-iterator" isn't really the buffer-size axis. **Any box can have many tasks**. A non-iterator downstream of an iterator runs as many times as the iterator fires its branch. Its output gets pushed downstream that many times.

So buffer-size analysis is really: "how many task invocations of the producer box, and how many of the consumer box, and what's the worst-case backlog at the slot." Iterator-fed is the most common case where N>1, but not the only one. I'll restate 302 to use the "box invocation count" framing.

## 2. 1-cell vs N-cell

`n_cells` is the number of cells in the ring buffer — i.e., how many distinct values the slot can hold simultaneously. `cell_capacity` is the size in bytes of a single cell. A 1-cell slot holds one value (single-value); an N-cell slot is a queue with N positions.

The *read mode* (peek vs pop) was historically tied to capacity in the design — 1-cell peek, N-cell pop. They're orthogonal in principle, but coupling them simplifies the API: if you need to keep a value around, allocate 1-cell + peek; if you need a queue, allocate N-cell + pop.

## 3. Counter approach + functional alternative

Functional alternative I considered: an iterator is a regular box with two inputs — `value` and `counter` — where `counter` is fed by a separate "counter generator" box. The counter generator self-loops: takes its previous output as input, emits previous+1. The iterator routes `value` to `outputs[counter % N]`. No iterator-internal state, fully data-driven.

Why I'd still go with per-box counter for our case: the functional version **serializes counter generation** through the counter box's tasks. Each counter task depends on the previous via the self-loop. To parallelize iterator invocations you'd need the counter box to pre-emit faster than consumers drain, which essentially requires a separate scheduling discipline for the counter box.

The per-box-counter-with-atomic-increment-at-spawn version gets parallelism for free: at task spawn, atomic fetch-and-add on the counter, snapshot into the task. Sibling iterator tasks run on different workers with independent counter values. Counter is a single int + atomic op per spawn.

So I'd ship per-box counter with atomic spawn-time increment, but I'll note the functional alternative in 304 as a documented trade-off for future reconsideration if it ever bites.

## 4. Parallel iterator execution — yes, achievable

With atomic spawn-time counter increment, iterator tasks can run in parallel. The race that's left is **push ordering at the consumer**: if iterator A's tasks 5 and 6 run on different workers, task 6 might push to consumer C first.

Solution: **each push carries a tag** equal to the source iterator's counter at task-spawn time. Consumer slots become tag-ordered (priority queue): pop returns the lowest-tag value, not the head value. For non-iterator producers, tag is always 0 (or omitted); FIFO falls out for free.

Cost: ~4-8 bytes per cell for the tag field. Slot pop becomes O(log n) instead of O(1) for tag-ordered slots. Compile-time analysis tags only the slots that need ordering (downstream of iterators, in branches that preserve order).

This restores deterministic pairing and lets iterator tasks parallelize. It's the "indexed pairing" follow-on, but for "phase 3 as designed" we should pull it forward. Worth specifying now, not later.

## 5. Now updating the issues

Let me start with the search.

Each slot is a ring buffer; `n_cells = 1` for single-output, `n_cells > 1` for queued inputs. Reference counted; producers and consumers all hold refs while alive. Variable-size payloads use a separate large-value heap with handles in the slot.
13	- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded by the runner via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t` interface (init / teardown / compile / invoke). No language is privileged — Lua, C, and Bash are reference implementations on equal footing.

15	- **Dispatch layer** (issue 304) is the worker-side action: read inputs from slots → invoke the language spec (or route, for comparators / iterators) → write output → unref consumed inputs → fire connections.
16	- **Iterator and comparator routing** lives entirely in the dispatch layer. No spec is invoked for those box kinds.
17	- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program. No retry, no fallback, no failure propagation.
18	- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations (sleep, blocking I/O) tie up a worker thread for the duration. Pool size is the budget for concurrent blocking activities. Cooperative pattern at graph level (split kick-off + check-done through an iterator with queued input) avoids holding a worker. Documented in `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.
19	
20	**Effil is explicitly NOT used** and is removed from all docs and issues. The 3d-rts pool is the chosen mechanism. Coroutines were considered as an intermediate stage but dropped in favor of going straight from sync to pool.
21	
22	**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the C pool runner with `lang_spec_t` and the slot store. 37	## Intended behavior
38	
39	### Pool source
40	The thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at
41	`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`
42	(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not
43	symlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts
44	working tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`
45	and `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.
46	
47	### Where the pool lives in the process
48	The pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map
49	run. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and
50	destroyed after the run completes.
51	
52	The C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):
53	
54	```c
55	int main(int argc, char **argv) {
56	    // 1. parse map path from argv
57	    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)
58	    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses
59	    // 4. pool = pool_create(n_workers)
60	    // 5. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present
61	    // 6. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes
62	    // 7. wait for active task count to reach zero
63	    // 8. pool_destroy(pool)
64	    // 9. write last-run.json
65	}
66	```
67	
68	### Graph loading: ported to C
69	The graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives
70	inside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no
71	embedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small
72	vendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to
73	implementation).
74	
75	Lua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even
76	then, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool
77	runner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.
78	
79	### Per-worker language runtimes
80	No language is treated as the "native" or preferred language at the
81	thread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the
82	same task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's
83	invocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.
84	
85	Each worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per
86	language it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool
87	startup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:
88	
89	```c
90	typedef struct {
91	    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state
92	    int     thread_idx;
93	} worker_ctx_t;
94	```
95	
96	Only the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.
97	If the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any
98	worker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and
99	passes that set to the pool runner at startup.
100	
101	The per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language
102	runtime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`
103	function at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.
104	
105	### Worker context access
106	Worker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread
107	worker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after
108	the thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.
109	
110	### Pool size
111	Number of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs
112	(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum
113	(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment
114	variable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.
115	
116	### Slots are owned by tasks (issue 302)
117	Slots are allocated when a task is created, not pre-allocated at
118	startup. A task allocates its output slot(s) at submission time, with
119	size specified by the task's language and function. The pool runner
120	does not own a slot region — slots are per-task allocations that
121	outlive the task only as long as wires hold references to them. See
122	issue 302 for the slot lifecycle.
123	
124	### Quiescence
125	The runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`
126	and decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits
```

```
60	### All slots are ring buffers
61	
62	There is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,
63	each of `cell_capacity` bytes. Every input port has a ring buffer
64	of compile-time-determined size:
65	
66	- **Default size**: enough cells to absorb the maximum number of
67	  pushes that can happen before the box can drain. For a port fed
68	  by a single non-iterator producer, that's 1. For a port fed by
69	  an iterator, it's the iterator's worst-case backlog (statically
70	  inferred or capped at a high default like 64 with growth).
71	- **Upper bound**: lists grow if backlog exceeds the pre-allocated
72	  size, so n_cells isn't a hard cap on correctness — only on
73	  pre-allocation efficiency.
74	
75	The producer pushes one cell per fan-out path; the consumer pops
76	one cell per invocation. Fan-in is multiple producers pushing into
77	the same input slot in arrival order; the consumer pops in FIFO
78	order.
79	
80	### Asynchrony
81	The store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and
82	freed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization
83	is per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.
84	
85	## Slot layout
86	
87	Each slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`
88	bytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:
89	
90	```
91	Slot header
92	Offset  Size  Field
93	------  ----  -----
94	0       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)
95	4       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation)
96	8       4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)
97	12      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)
98	16      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)
99	17      3     _pad
100	20      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))
101	```
102	
103	Each cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`
104	bytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across
105	slots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing
106	sizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows
107	how big it needs the cells.
108	
109	`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation
110	(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`
111	spins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —
112	if contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without
113	changing the API.
114	
115	Writes to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is
116	advanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to
117	see the complete value at the head cell.
118	
119	## Lifetime and end-of-stream
120	
121	Slots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live
122	from graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference
123	counting — the slot is freed when the run ends, alongside its
124	owning box.
125	
126	### End-of-stream detection (replacing producer refcounts)
127	
128	Each slot tracks the set of upstream producer boxes that may still
129	push into it. When a producer's "no more pushes" condition fires
130	— either it has finished all its invocations, or it transitively
131	depends only on producers that have finished — the dispatch layer
132	removes that producer from the slot's producer set.
133	
134	When the producer set is empty AND the slot's queue is drained,
135	the consumer box has reached end-of-stream on that port. For an
136	iterator, this is what tells the iterator to stop re-spawning. For
137	a non-iterator, this means no further invocations are coming;
138	combined with the same condition on its other input ports, the
139	box itself is done.
140	
141	This replaces the per-slot refcount machinery. The "are upstreams
142	still alive" check is done at the producer-set level, which is
143	cheaper and avoids the contention of refcount churn on hot paths.
144	
145	### No wait lists
146	
147	Tasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch
148	layer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they
149	never block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the
150	spawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,
151	no per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.
152	
153	## Backing store
154	
155	Slots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a
156	per-run allocator (described under "Allocation strategy" below) that
157	hands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is
158	sufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write
159	it, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.
```

28	## Task struct
29	
30	A task is one ephemeral invocation of a box. Its struct carries
31	just enough to point the action at the box and the snapshot of its
32	counter at spawn time:
33	
34	```c
35	typedef struct {
36	    int  box_id;          // index into the graph's box array
37	    int  counter;         // iterator only; snapshot at spawn time
38	} dispatch_task_t;
39	```
40	
41	There is no `input_slots` array on the task — the box's input
42	slots are durable per-box state (see issue 302). The action looks
43	up the input and output slots through `box_runtime_state[box_id]`.
44	
45	There is no `output_slot` either — output is a routing event, not
46	a stored value. When the action finishes, it pushes copies of the
47	return value into the input slots of every downstream box wired
48	to this output (and only the matching branch for comparators and
49	iterators).
50	
51	Tasks are spawned by the dispatch layer's "spawn on input ready"
52	rule (issue 302). Each spawn allocates a fresh `dispatch_task_t`
53	on the pool's task allocator, pre-populated with the box ID and
54	counter value. The action's first read of the input slots is what
55	drains them — pop one cell per input port.
56	
57	## The dispatch action
58	
59	```c
60	action_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);
61	```
62	
63	Phases, in order:
64	
65	### 1. Read inputs into byte buffers
66	
67	Tasks are spawned only when every input port has at least one
68	value (issue 302's spawn-on-input-ready rule), so the action does
69	not need to check or block — input availability is the spawn
70	precondition.
71	
72	For each input port: `slot_pop` from the box's input slot into a
73	heap-allocated buffer sized to the slot's `cell_capacity`. Pop
74	drains one cell from the front of the ring; subsequent values
75	behind it are still queued and will spawn further tasks.
76	
77	Variable-size payloads work via the large-value heap (issue 302):
78	the popped cell holds a `{size, offset}` handle that points into
79	the heap; the spec follows the handle if it needs the bytes.
80	
81	Buffers are freed when the action ends.
82	
83	### 3. Dispatch by box mode
84	The action now branches on the box's mode:
85	
86	- **Plain call box**: proceed to phase 4 (invoke) and phase 5 (write
87	  output) as below.
```

170	### 7. Post-action: counter advancement (iterators only)
171	
172	Routing already happened in phase 5 — pushes targeted the right
173	downstream input slots based on the box's mode. The remaining
174	post-action work is iterator-specific:
175	
176	- **Iterator**: increment `box_runtime_state[box_id].counter`
177	  modulo `n_iter_outputs`. The next iterator task spawned for this
178	  box (when its input slot has another value) will read the
179	  updated counter value from the box state.
180	
181	There is no "successor task" spawned by the iterator itself. The
182	spawn-on-input-ready rule in issue 302 handles iterator
183	re-invocation the same way it handles every other box: the
184	iterator's input slot has further values queued, the spawn rule
185	fires again automatically.
186	
187	Plain call and comparator boxes do nothing in phase 7.
188	
189	### 8. Return ACT_DONE
190	The action completes. The pool decrements the active-task counter
191	(issue 301). If the counter reaches zero and the runner is waiting,
192	the run ends.
193	
194	## Initial submission
195	
196	At startup, the pool runner walks the graph and pushes the
197	literal-input values (from `value` fields on input ports) directly
198	into the corresponding input slots. Boxes whose input set becomes
199	fully populated by literals — entry-point boxes — immediately
200	satisfy the spawn-on-input-ready condition, and their first task
201	gets queued. From there, every subsequent task spawn follows from
202	the regular phase-5 push → spawn-check chain.
203	
204	Iterator counter state starts at 0; literal-only entry iterators
205	spawn their first task at startup and increment from there.
206	
207	## Cross-iterator pairing
208	
209	When a non-iterator consumer C has two input ports wired from two
210	different iterators A and B, each input port has its own queue.
211	Tasks for C spawn FIFO: task 1 pops the first value from each
212	queue; task 2 pops the second from each; etc.
213	
214	Pairing is deterministic **as long as A and B push in deterministic
215	order**. In a single-threaded run that's automatic. In a parallel
216	run where A and B run on different workers and push concurrently,
217	the pairing depends on push ordering — which is non-deterministic
218	across runs.
219	
220	For phase 3, FIFO pairing is the policy. If a workload needs
221	strict pairing (a_i with b_i regardless of push race), the right
222	fix is per-invocation index tags on the values: each iterator
223	push tags its value with its counter, the consumer's queues sort
224	by tag before popping. That's a follow-on issue (no number yet),
225	opened only if a real workload needs it.
226	
227	## Comparator vs iterator vs plain call
228	
229	Three box modes drive routing differently:
230	
231	| Mode        | Output kind   | Invoke spec? | Routing behavior                                                    |
232	|-------------|---------------|--------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
233	| Plain call  | single value  | yes          | fire all outgoing connections                                       |
234	| Comparator  | passthrough   | no           | dispatch layer compares input to threshold, fires lt / eq / gt only |

55	### Phase 3 runner — `soramech-pool` (planned, issues 301–311)
56	
57	C binary that owns a 3d-rts thread pool. Each box invocation is a
58	pool task; worker threads run them concurrently. Language code is
59	called through **language specs** (issue 303), shared libraries
60	(`langs/<name>/spec.so`) loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Lua and C
61	specs are in-process; the Bash spec talks to a persistent subprocess
62	over a Unix domain socket. Wire values live in **slots** in process
63	heap memory (issue 302) — fixed-size with reference counting, plus a
64	large-value heap for variable-size payloads.
65	
66	Phase 3 replaces the phase 2 runner wholesale. The synchronous path
67	does not survive into phase 3; the editor and the map directory
68	format are unchanged across the cutover.

226	## Execution model — phase 3 (thread pool)
227	
228	The C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool with N worker threads.
229	Each box invocation is a task. The dispatch layer (issue 304) is the
230	worker-side action: read inputs from slots → invoke the language
231	spec (or route, for comparators / iterators) → write output to a
232	slot → unref consumed inputs → fire downstream connections.
233	
234	Slots are per-task ring buffers with reference-counted lifetime
235	(issue 302). Wires hold references; producers push, consumers peek
236	or pop. The wait list on each slot is the synchronization primitive
237	that parks blocked tasks until a producer fills the slot.
238	
239	The pool runner has no embedded Lua. It is C from `main` down to the
240	language spec boundary; only inside a Lua spec's `invoke` does Lua
241	code run, and only inside that worker's `lua_State`. The graph
242	loader is also pure C (issue 305) — phase 2's
243	`src/003-loader.lua` retires.
244	
245	See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` for the full IPC and threading
246	discussion, including the blocking-semantics constraint on long-
247	running operations.
248	
249	## Data files
250	
251	Persistent data lives in `data/<name>.json`. Format:
252	
253	```json
254	{
255	  "constant": false,
256	  "fields": {
257	    "history": [],
258	    "config": { "constant": true, "value": { "model": "soramind-default" } }
259	  }

20	A top-level `Makefile` at the project root orchestrates the entire
21	phase 3 build. It builds:
22	
23	1. The pool runner binary: `soramech-pool` (statically links the
24	   3d-rts task pool, the vendored JSON parser, the slot store, the
25	   graph loader, the dispatch layer, the spec registry).
26	2. Each language spec: `langs/<name>/spec.so`, built by a small
27	   per-spec Makefile.
28	3. (Optional) Unit test binaries.
29	
30	Each component has its own Makefile if it has non-trivial build
31	rules. The top-level Makefile delegates to them via `$(MAKE) -C
32	<dir>`. A clean checkout becomes a working build with `make`.
33	
34	## Directory layout
35	
36	```
37	soramech/
38	├── Makefile                       ← top-level orchestration
39	├── soramech-pool                  ← built binary (gitignored)
40	├── src/
41	│   ├── 008-pool-runner.c          ← main entry, pool lifecycle (issue 301)
42	│   ├── slot-store.c / .h          ← per-task slot allocator (issue 302)
43	│   ├── graph-loader.c / .h        ← C loader, replaces 003-loader.lua (issue 305)
44	│   ├── dispatch.c / .h            ← dispatch action (issue 304)
45	│   └── spec-registry.c / .h       ← spec dlopen/registry (issue 303)
46	├── libs/
47	│   ├── task-pool/                 ← vendored 3d-rts pool
48	│   │   ├── 900-task-pool.h
49	│   │   └── 900-task-pool.c
50	│   └── json/                      ← vendored JSON parser (cJSON, jsmn, etc.)
51	│       ├── cjson.h
52	│       └── cjson.c
53	├── langs/
54	│   ├── lua/

6	## Current behavior
7	The 3d-rts task pool's `pool_spawn` takes a priority parameter:
8	
9	```c
10	task_id_t pool_spawn(task_pool_t *pool,
11	                     action_fn_t  *actions,
12	                     void        **action_args,
13	                     int           n_actions,
14	                     int           priority);
15	```
16	
17	Higher priority tasks are dispatched ahead of lower priority tasks
18	when multiple are ready. The pool's queue handles the ordering.
19	
20	Phase 3 needs to specify what SoraMech does with this knob. The
21	simplest answer is the right one for now: do nothing.
22	
23	## Decision
24	
25	Every dispatch task is submitted at priority `1`. The compile-time
26	constant `MAX_PRIORITY` is set to `1`. There is no graph-level or
27	box-level concept of priority. The runner does not expose any user-
28	facing knob for it.
29	
30	The mechanism is wired through the codebase — every `pool_spawn`
```

Slot ownership pointer corrected to per-input-port.

**Issue 302**: 1-cell peek + N-cell pop distinction restored. Compile-time wire classification (runs-once → 1-cell peek, runs-N-times → N-cell pop) drives slot allocation. Cell tagging support added — cells carry a 4-byte ordering tag, tagged slots `slot_pop` returns the lowest-tag cell. Slot lifetime simplified: durable for the run, no refcounting, no producer-set, no wait list. The `slot_alloc` API gains a `flags` argument (e.g., `SLOT_TAGGED`); `slot_push` gains a tag parameter (zero for untagged).

  2. 1-cell vs N-cell

  n_cells is the number of cells in the ring buffer — i.e., how many distinct values the slot can hold simultaneously. cell_capacity is the
  size in bytes of a single cell. A 1-cell slot holds one value (single-value); an N-cell slot is a queue with N positions.

  The read mode (peek vs pop) was historically tied to capacity in the design — 1-cell peek, N-cell pop. They're orthogonal in principle, but
   coupling them simplifies the API: if you need to keep a value around, allocate 1-cell + peek; if you need a queue, allocate N-cell + pop.

Let me work through both threads.

## Self-push counter

The design works:

```
Iterator box (call type)
  Inputs:
    value    (from upstream, N-cell pop slot)
    counter  (self-loop, N-cell pop slot, primed with 0 at startup)
  Outputs (N branches)
    output_0, output_1, ... output_{N-1}
    next_counter (self-loop wire back to counter input)

Per invocation:
  pop value, pop counter
  route value to outputs[counter % N]
  push (counter + 1) to next_counter
```

Counter is data, not box state. Conceptually clean — the iterator becomes a regular call box that happens to self-loop one of its outputs.

**The catch you already identified**: tasks serialize through the counter dependency. Task K can't spawn until task K-1 has pushed counter=K. Even though we accept non-deterministic routing, the dispatch chain is still single-file because no task has its counter input ready until the previous one finishes. So we lose the parallelism the atomic-fetch-add design buys.

You said "we make no guarantees that inputs will route to output ports in a deterministic way" — that's about *which* branch a value goes to, not about whether tasks run in parallel. Even with ordering-relaxed semantics, the counter input being a single-stream queue forces serial execution.

To get parallelism with the self-push design, the counter input would need to be **pre-populated** with multiple values upfront (so task 0, 1, 2 can all spawn immediately). That requires knowing N at compile time, which we don't.

So: self-push is the cleaner design conceptually, atomic-fetch-add is the better design for performance. Given high-performance is a stated goal, I'd stick with atomic-fetch-add. Functional purity isn't worth losing core-scaling.

## Merging iterator and comparator

There are three levels at which they could merge. Worth picking explicitly.

### Level A — Mental-model unification only

Both are "branching boxes" in the editor and docs. Same conceptual category: "this box has multiple output branches, only one fires per invocation, the box's settings decide which." Comparator and iterator are two presets under that umbrella. Editor UI groups them. Runtime keeps them as separate dispatch-action paths.

Cost: zero code change.
Win: clearer narrative for users learning the editor.

### Level B — Unified router schema, separate dispatch paths

A box has a `routing` field:

```json
{ "routing": { "kind": "comparator", "comparand": 4 } }
{ "routing": { "kind": "iterator",   "outputs": ["a","b","c"] } }
```

Both kinds carry their own params; the dispatch layer reads `routing.kind` and branches into the appropriate code path. The schema is unified; the runtime isn't really.

Cost: small refactor (current `comparand` and `iterator_outputs` move under `routing`). Editor UI consolidates.
Win: one place to add routing kinds (e.g., user-defined router via spec callback), one place for compile validation.

### Level C — One unified dispatch path

A "router" abstraction at the dispatch layer:

```
Dispatch action for a router box:
  1. (optional) Invoke spec on inputs → returns value (and possibly a branch hint)
  2. Compute branch via routing_rule:
       - "comparand"        → compare(value, params.comparand) → lt/eq/gt
       - "counter"          → params.counter++ % N → output_K
       - "function_return"  → spec returned (value, branch); use branch
       - "fan_all"          → no branch, fire all (= plain call)
  3. Push value (or popped input, for counter-mode without spec) to selected branch(es)
```

Box modes become routing-rule values:
- Plain call → `"fan_all"`
- Comparator → spec runs + `"comparand"` rule
- Iterator → no spec + `"counter"` rule
- (New) Function-decided routing → spec runs + `"function_return"` rule

Cost: real refactor. Dispatch-action code consolidated. Spec interface grows a way for `invoke` to return a branch tag (already on the table for "function-defined routing" anyway).
Win: future routing kinds slot in cleanly. Iterator-with-function (your "functions iterating their own outputs") becomes natural — just a router with both spec and counter rule, or with `function_return` rule.

### Recommendation

I'd ship **Level B now**, queue **Level C** for after phase 3 ships. Level B is a small refactor, makes the schema coherent, and sets up Level C cleanly. Level C is the right end-state but requires settling the spec-returns-branch contract, which is a bigger commit.

Level A happens for free as part of B (the doc reframes naturally).

Want me to:
1. Open an issue for Level B (the schema unification)?
2. Add Level C as a planned-but-deferred follow-on?

Or pick a different path through this?

That's a clean fix. Let me describe what it solves, then ship the changes.

## Atomic-counter slot — yes, this works

A new slot mode that's just "an atomic int with a special read op":

```c
// Allocated with SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER flag
slot_alloc(store, /*cell_capacity*/ 4, /*n_cells*/ 1, SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER);

// Read-and-increment, atomic
int slot_read_inc(store, slot_id, int mod);
// equivalent to:
//   uint32_t v = atomic_fetch_add(&slot->cell[0].data, 1);
//   return v % mod;
```

From the outside: a regular slot. Consumers see a slot value that moves; they don't see the box state. Concurrent readers each get a unique value because of the atomic fetch-add. No push needed; the read is the increment.

The iterator box's dispatch action becomes:
```
1. Pop value from value-input slot.
2. branch_idx = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs);
3. Push value to outputs[branch_idx], with tag=branch_idx
4. Done.
```

Counter lives in a slot, not in `box_runtime_state`. Iterators don't have any per-box mutable state — they're just a routing rule plus a designated atomic-counter slot. Parallel iterator tasks all read from the same atomic slot independently; each gets a unique value. Counter overflow wraps mod N gracefully.

The slot store knows about this read mode (it owns the atomic primitive); the dispatch layer just calls `slot_read_inc`. The spec never sees any of it.

This unifies nicely: atomic-counter slots are a building block that any feature needing "thread-safe sequence" can use, not just iterators.

The atomic\nfetch-add means concurrent spawns get distinct counter values, so\n**iterator tasks can run in parallel** on different workers — each\nhas its own counter, picks its own output branch independently.\nSibling iterator tasks don't share runtime state.\n\nThe serial dependency is reduced to one atomic op per spawn (cheap)\nrather than a serialized task chain.\n\n## Cross-iterator pairing under parallel iteration\n\nWith parallel iterator tasks, push ordering at the consumer is\nnon-deterministic — task 6 of iterator A may push to consumer C\nbefore task 5 if 6 happened to land on a faster worker. FIFO pop\nat C would consume them out of iteration order.\n\nThe fix is **counter-tagged pushes**. Each iterator push (in phase\n5) carries the counter value snapshotted at spawn:\n\n```c\nslot_push(downstream.input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n          /* tag = */ task->counter);\n```"

Done. Summary:

**Atomic-counter slot** — added to 302 as `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` mode + `slot_read_inc(slot, mod)` op. The slot's "cell" is just an atomic uint32 under the hood; the read op atomically fetches-and-adds, returns mod N. Iterator counter moves into this slot; box state loses its `counter` field. Iterators now parallel by default — concurrent `slot_read_inc` calls give each task a unique routing index.

**304** updated to read counter via `slot_read_inc` mid-action rather than at spawn. Task struct shrinks to just `{ box_id }` — no per-task counter snapshot needed because the slot itself is the source of truth.

**Issue 233** opened for Level B: unified `routing: { kind, ... }` field replacing separate `comparand` and `iterator_outputs`. Includes:
- Schema migration plan for legacy maps (loader-side, transparent).
- Inspector `mode` dropdown replacing the two separate toggles.
- An open question about function-backed iterators (recommendation: support; the dispatch flow naturally accommodates "function runs, output gets routed" for both comparator and iterator).
- Level C explicitly noted as deferred follow-on.

Spec interface stays clean — the spec sees only `invoke(bytes_in) → bytes_out`, no awareness of routing or branches. Routing decisions are dispatch-layer concerns; counter values are slot-store concerns. The user-facing concept of "branching boxes" is editor + map-file knowledge.

Where do you want to go next? Implementation order of phase 2 issues we've opened (229, 230, 231, 233), or another design thread to chase?

With `thresholds: [4]` this becomes the current\n3-branch lt/eq/gt (with `eq` being \"exactly 4\"), so the legacy\nshape is one configuration of the new one.\n\nEquality cases (`x == 3` exactly) fall to the lower band by\nconvention; an explicit `eq` band could be added per threshold\nif needed.\n\nDefer the schema specifics — the existing 3-branch case ships\nfirst; multi-band is a follow-on once we have a use case that\nactually needs more than three.\n\n### kind=\"iterator\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\n`n_outputs` output ports, named conventionally (`out_0`, `out_1`,\n…). Every invocation reads the box's `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot\nvia `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)`; that index picks\nthe branch.\n\nThe function still runs and produces the routed value. Iterator\ndefaults the function to a passthrough identity if the user\nhasn't picked a `ref` / `fn` — but the user is free to attach\nany function whose output should be round-robin-distributed.\n\n### kind=\"randomizer\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"randomizer\", \"n_outputs\": 4 }\n```\n\nPicks a branch uniformly at random per invocation.\nImplementation: hash the counter-slot value into the branch\nindex, so the distribution is deterministic-given-seed but\nspread across branches.\n\n```c\nuint32_t i = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, UINT32_MAX);\nuint32_t branch = hash(i) % n_outputs;\n```\n\n`hash` is a cheap mixing function (xorshift, FNV); not\ncryptographic. The point is breaking up the monotonic counter so\nconsecutive calls don't go to consecutive branches.\n\n### kind=\"weighted\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":    \"weighted\",\n  \"weights\": [0.8, 0.2]\n}\n```\n\nProbability-based distribution. With `[0.8, 0.2]` and two output\nports, 80% of invocations fire branch 0, 20% fire branch 1.\n\nImplementation: at compile time, weights are normalized into a\ncumulative table on a `0..PRECISION-1` integer scale (e.g.\n`PRECISION = 1000`). Per call:\n\n```c\nuint32_t r = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, PRECISION);\n// pre-computed cumulative: [0..799] → branch 0, [800..999] → branch 1\nuint32_t branch = lookup_band(r, cumulative_table);\n```\n\nSame counter-slot machinery as iterator and randomizer; the\ndifference is the mapping from counter to branch.\n\n### kind=\"distributor\" (load-aware)\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\nSends the value to the **least-busy** downstream consumer:\ninspects the fill levels of the input slots wired to each branch\nand picks the branch whose downstream slot has the fewest queued\nvalues.\n\nImplementation: dispatch action peeks the `tail - head` count on\neach downstream input slot and picks the minimum. Tied branches\nfall back to atomic-counter round-robin so ties don't always go\nto the same branch.\n\nThis is the only routing kind that's not purely\nself-contained — it reads downstream slot state — but it doesn't\nadd any new dispatch-layer concept beyond querying slot fill\n(which the slot store already knows).\n\n### Future kinds\n\nThe pattern is: any new routing kind plugs in at one place\n(`routing.kind` value + dispatch-layer branch picker). All\nexisting kinds and any future ones live entirely in the dispatch\nlayer + slot store + editor — never in language specs, never in\nuser-written functions.\n\n## Iterator + function: ships as \"function always runs\"\n\nIterator boxes always run their function. The dispatch action\nbecomes uniform across routing kinds:\n\n```\n1. Read inputs (pop / peek per port mode).\n2. Invoke spec (always — function runs regardless of routing kind).\n3. Pick branch via routing.kind:\n     comparator   → compare(output, comparand)\n     iterator     → slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)\n     randomizer   → hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % n_outputs\n     weighted     → cumulative lookup\n     distributor  → argmin(downstream fill)\n     (no routing) → fan to all outgoing wires\n4. Push function output to outputs[picked branch] (or all wires if\n   no routing).\n```\n\nA single dispatch path for all branching boxes; the routing rule\nplugs into step 3.\n\n## Schema migration\n\nFew enough existing maps that we can hand-migrate them. The\nloader does **not** carry a legacy-shape adapter; once this\nships, all map files are expected to use the `routing` field. If\na map with the old shape is opened, the schema validator rejects\nit and the user (or a one-off migration script) updates it.\n\nIf we end up wanting a one-off script, it walks `maps/<name>/boxes/*.json`\nand rewrites:\n- `comparand: X` → `routing: { kind: \"comparator\", comparand: X }`\n- `iterator_outputs: [...]` → `routing: { kind: \"iterator\", n_outputs: len(...) }`\n- everything else → no change\n\nBut for the current map count, manual edits are faster than\nwriting the script.\n\n## Inspector UI\n\nA `routing` selector in the inspector replaces the separate\n`compare` toggle and `iterator` toggle:\n\n```\nmode:    [plain ▾ | comparator | iterator | randomizer | weighted | distributor]\n```\n\nPer-kind controls below the dropdown:\n- **plain**: nothing extra.\n- **comparator**: numeric `comparand` input. (Multi-band UI is\n  the brainstorm above; ships single-threshold first.)\n- **iterator**: `n_outputs` integer input.\n- **randomizer**: `n_outputs` integer input.\n- **weighted**: editable list of weight values (one per output);\n  N derived from list length.\n- **distributor**: `n_outputs` integer input.\n\nOutput ports re-render to match the routing kind: 1 dot for\nplain, 3 fixed dots (lt/eq/gt) for comparator, N dots for the\ncounter-based kinds. Port names follow the routing kind's\nconvention; not user-renameable (issue 224's read-only-port-name\nrule).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua`: accept `routing` field; reject legacy\n   `comparand` and `iterator_outputs` shapes.\n2. `assets/js/004-inspector.js`: mode dropdown replacing the two\n   toggles; per-kind controls.\n3. `assets/js/002-boxes.js`: render branches based on\n   `routing.kind`.\n4. `assets/js/006-wires.js`: connection's `from_branch` matches\n   the routing kind's port naming.\n5. Phase 3 dispatch (issue 304): branch on `routing.kind` for the\n   branch-selection step. Five rule paths (one per kind shipped),\n   plus the no-routing-field plain path.\n\nHand-migrate existing maps before merging.\n\n## Why now\n\n- Editor inspector keeps gaining toggles per routing kind. A\n  unified mode dropdown scales linearly with kinds; separate\n  toggles don't.\n- Phase 3 dispatch will naturally have a \"select branch\" step;\n  routing it through `routing.kind` is the same code regardless\n  of whether we ship Level B now or refactor later.\n- The new routing kinds (randomizer, weighted, distributor) only\n  make sense in the unified schema. Adding them as separate\n  top-level fields would be unmaintainable.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — schema accepts new field\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — mode dropdown\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — branch rendering\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — branch matching\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — counter slot mechanism\n  used by iterator / randomizer / weighted\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer's branch\n  picker dispatches on `routing.kind`\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Distributor under fan-out**: if a branch wire goes to\n  multiple consumers (fan-out), the \"fill level\" of that branch\n  is ambiguous. Use the max of the consumers' fills, or the sum,\n  or something else. Probably max — the bottleneck is the\n  slowest consumer.\n- **Multi-band comparator threshold edges**: `x == threshold`\n  goes to which side of the cut? Lean toward \"less-than-or-equal\"\n  for consistency. Need to nail down before implementation.\n- **Weighted ties**: floating-point weights summing to `1.0`\n  doesn't always discretize cleanly. Compile-time normalization\n  picks an integer scale (1000) and rounds; the last band\n  absorbs any leftover so the ranges always sum to PRECISION.\n\n## Level C example (deferred)\n\nThe big follow-on after this issue ships is a fully data-driven\nrouter: one dispatch path that reads a small rule expression\nfrom the box JSON and evaluates it. Example shape:\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\": \"rules\",\n  \"rules\": [\n    { \"when\": \"output < 3\",                   \"to\": \"small\" },\n    { \"when\": \"output >= 3 and output < 7\",   \"to\": \"medium\" },\n    { \"when\": \"output >= 7\",                  \"to\": \"large\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nThe dispatch layer ships a small expression evaluator (a few\ndozen lines: variables = `output`, `counter`, `fill[i]`;\noperators = comparisons, boolean conjunction, arithmetic). Every\nexisting routing kind reduces to a \"rules\" expression:\n\n- comparator → three rules with `when: output < c / output == c / output > c`\n- iterator → one rule using `counter % N` as the band index\n- randomizer → one rule using `hash(counter) % N`\n- weighted → cumulative-band rules\n\nThe benefit: one code path in dispatch instead of five. Custom\nrouting without writing a spec callback or modifying user\nfunctions. 141	### 5. Write output (push to downstream input slots)
142	
143	Output is a routing event. The action walks the box's outgoing
144	connection list and calls `slot_push(downstream.input_slot,
145	output_buf, output_size)` for each one — copying the output bytes
146	into every consumer's input slot.
147	
148	For comparator boxes: only push to the connection whose
149	`from_branch` matches the lt/eq/gt result. For iterator boxes:
150	only push to the connection whose `from_branch` matches
151	`iterator_outputs[counter]`.
152	
153	After each push, the spawn-on-input-ready check (issue 302) fires
154	on the receiving box. If that push completes its input set, a
155	fresh task spawns for the consumer.
156	
157	### 6. (No phase 6)
158	
159	Slots are durable for the run; tasks don't unref. Run termination
160	is governed by the pool's active-task counter (issue 301). The
161	dispatch action goes from phase 5 directly to phase 7.
162	
163	### 7. Post-action: nothing for the action itself
164	
165	Routing happened in phase 5. The iterator counter was already
166	incremented at task **spawn** time, not here — the spawn-time
167	atomic increment is what makes parallel iterator tasks possible
168	(see "Iterator counter and parallel iteration" below). All boxes
169	do nothing in phase 7.

259	## Comparator vs iterator vs plain call
260	
261	Three box modes drive routing differently:
262	
263	| Mode        | Output kind   | Invoke spec? | Routing behavior                                                    |
264	|-------------|---------------|--------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
265	| Plain call  | single value  | yes          | fire all outgoing connections                                       |
266	| Comparator  | passthrough   | no           | dispatch layer compares input to threshold, fires lt / eq / gt only |
267	| Iterator    | passthrough   | no           | fire connection matching counter, increment counter, re-spawn       |
268	
269	The dispatch action branches on box mode early (phase 3) and
270	dispatches into the appropriate helper. Three small functions, not a
271	single switch, keep each mode's logic isolated.

279	  large-value heap (issue 302).

**Iterator runs its function** — no more "iterator passes input through unchanged" option. Every branching box runs its function; the routing kind only picks where the function's output goes. The ticket reads this as the canonical single behavior, not as one of two options.

**Dropped speculative kinds** — `function_decided` and `user_router` are gone. Both leaked language-spec or function-author concerns into the routing layer; they violate "routing logic is dispatch + editor only, never spec."

**New kinds added per your brainstorm**:

- `weighted` — user-defined percentages per branch (e.g., `[0.8, 0.2]`); compile-time normalized to a cumulative band table; lookup against the counter scaled to a 1000-step precision.
- `distributor` — argmin over downstream slot fill levels. Sends to the least-busy branch. Ties fall back to round-robin.
